Smoking lowers HDL, the particles that carry cholesterol to the liver, so more cholesterol clogs arteries; and it raises blood pressure, whose rapid, turbulent flow damages artery walls and makes them prone to cholesterol deposits, inflammation and so atherosclerosis.

1Ch. 12ashort answer12a.2 Thrombus and embolism
  • textbook
  • lecture

Compare and contrast a thrombus and an embolism, and explain how the place where a clot lodges decides the outcome.

Model answer

Both involve a blood clot in the wrong place. A thrombus is a stationary clot that forms on a vessel wall or in the heart — on the rough surface of a plaque, or in the deep leg veins when flow is sluggish — and it may block flow where it is. An embolism is a vessel blocked by a clot that broke free (often from a thrombus), travelled, and lodged in a smaller vessel, killing tissue beyond it. In the brain that is a stroke, in a coronary artery a heart attack, in the lungs a pulmonary embolism. Blood thinners (warfarin, heparin) prevent clots; t-PA dissolves a lodged one by activating plasmin.

Marks for: thrombus = formed and stays in place; embolism = drifted then lodged; the three sites and outcomes. The lecture words it as a circulating clot (embolus) that becomes a "thrombus" once caught — mention that if the question comes from lecture; the book's split above is the one that keeps the two distinct.

2Ch. 12ashort answer12a.3 Atherosclerosis
  • textbook

Describe how atherosclerosis develops, how HDL and LDL affect it, and what its complications are.

Model answer

An injury to the artery wall (smoke chemicals, cholesterol deposits, infection, turbulent high-pressure flow) makes the lining cells take up LDL. The LDL changes and triggers an inflammatory response: defense cells arrive, smooth muscle divides and thickens the wall, and LDL-filled defense cells form fatty streaks that grow into plaque. Plaque narrows the artery, or its fibrous cap ruptures and triggers a clot. Downstream tissue is starved: a heart attack in the coronary arteries (coronary artery disease, also angina), a stroke in the brain. LDL carries cholesterol to cells (bad); HDL carries it to the liver (good), so low LDL and high HDL mean low risk.

Marks for: injury → LDL → inflammation → plaque; rupture → clot; heart attack and stroke as complications; the direction each lipoprotein carries cholesterol.

3Ch. 12ashort answer12a.5 Smoking
  • textbook

Describe the effects of smoking on the cardiovascular system, specifically nicotine and carbon monoxide.

Model answer

Nicotine speeds the heart and constricts blood vessels, which raises blood pressure, and makes platelets stick together, so abnormal clots that cause heart attack or stroke are more likely. Carbon monoxide binds the red blood cells so they cannot carry oxygen — one cigarette cuts the blood's O2 capacity by about 12% — so less oxygen reaches the brain and heart and the heart has to work harder. Smoking also speeds atherosclerosis by lowering HDL and by raising blood pressure, whose turbulent flow damages artery walls.

Marks for: nicotine → higher BP and stickier platelets; CO → less oxygen carried, heart works harder; the link to atherosclerosis (lower HDL, damaged walls).

  • textbook

Thrombus

Back

A stationary clot formed on a vessel wall or in the heart; it may block flow where it sits.

2Ch. 12aflashcard12a.2 Thrombus and embolism
  • textbook

Embolism

Back

A vessel blocked by a clot that broke free, travelled and lodged; tissue beyond it dies (brain → stroke, heart → heart attack, lungs → pulmonary embolism).

3Ch. 12aflashcard12a.2 Treatment
  • textbook

Tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA)

Back

Drug that activates plasminogen to form plasmin, dissolving a lodged clot; give within 6 hours.

4Ch. 12aflashcard12a.3 High blood pressure
  • textbook
  • lecture

Hypertension

Back

High blood pressure, the "silent killer" — no telltale symptoms; enlarges the heart and damages brain, vessels and kidneys.

5Ch. 12aflashcard12a.3 Aneurysm
  • textbook
  • lecture

Aneurysm

Back

A weakened artery wall that balloons outward; it can burst (blood loss) or form clots. Common in the brain and the aorta.

6Ch. 12aflashcard12a.2 Thrombus and embolism
  • textbook
  • lecture

Stroke

Back

Brain tissue dies because its blood supply is cut off — by a lodged clot (embolism) or a burst vessel (ruptured aneurysm). Lecture: CVA.

7Ch. 12aflashcard12a.3 Atherosclerosis
  • textbook

Atherosclerosis

Back

Fatty plaque building up in artery walls, driven by inflammation after injury; narrows the artery and can rupture into a clot.

8Ch. 12aflashcard12a.3 Coronary artery disease
  • textbook

Coronary artery disease

Back

Atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries that feed the heart muscle; the cause of most heart attacks.

9Ch. 12aflashcard12a.3 Coronary artery disease
  • textbook
  • lecture

Angina (angina pectoris)

Back

Chest pain from a temporary O2 shortage to heart muscle; comes with exertion, stops with rest, no permanent damage.

10Ch. 12aflashcard12a.3 Coronary artery disease
  • textbook

Coronary angiography

Back

Diagnostic: catheter to the heart, dye into the coronary arteries, x-rays show narrowed areas.

11Ch. 12aflashcard12a.3 Surgery
  • textbook

Angioplasty

Back

A balloon on a catheter is inflated at the blockage, pressing plaque against the wall to widen the lumen.

12Ch. 12aflashcard12a.3 Surgery
  • textbook

Stent

Back

A metal-mesh tube left in the artery after angioplasty to keep it from collapsing; some release drugs.

13Ch. 12aflashcard12a.3 Surgery
  • textbook

Coronary bypass

Back

A piece of leg vein grafted from the aorta to a coronary artery, so blood goes around the blockage.

14Ch. 12aflashcard12a.4 Heart attack
  • textbook
  • lecture

Myocardial infarction

Back

A heart attack — heart muscle dies from too little blood; it is replaced by scar tissue that cannot contract.

15Ch. 12aflashcard12a.4 Heart attack
  • textbook

Coronary thrombosis

Back

A clot blocking a coronary artery — the most common cause of a heart attack; unlikely without plaque.

16Ch. 12aflashcard12a.4 Heart failure
  • textbook

Heart failure

Back

The damaged heart is no longer an efficient pump: breathlessness, fatigue, fluid in lungs or limbs. Digitalis strengthens contractions.

17Ch. 12aflashcard12a.3 Cholesterol
  • textbook

HDL vs LDL

Back

LDL ("bad") carries cholesterol to cells, where it deposits; HDL ("good") carries it to the liver for disposal.

Ch. 13 — Body Defense Mechanisms

Week 14 · study page · 63 multiple choice · 3 short answer · 43 flashcards

1Ch. 1313.8 · Autoimmune disorders
  • textbook

Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks cells in the joints. Which of these is most likely to make the immune system attack the body's own cells?

Answer: d

Lymphocytes are meant to tolerate self, and those that react to self are normally destroyed as they mature; in autoimmune disease some escape and attack the body's own tissues ("friendly fire"). T cells with no receptor (a) or that recognize nothing (c) could not target the joints at all, and with no T cells (b) there would be no attack.

2Ch. 1313.4 · Cell-mediated responses
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A disease destroys many of a patient's T cells. Which ability of the immune system would that most directly reduce?

Answer: b

Cytotoxic T cells kill infected body cells — the cell-mediated response — so losing T cells hits that job directly. The innate defenses (a) — barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, inflammation — do not depend on T cells. Antigen-presenting cells (c) are macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells, not T-cell products. Helper T cells activate B cells; they do not destroy them (d).

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

3Ch. 1313.2 · Inflammation
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A sprained ankle swells within the hour. Which event in the inflammatory response produces the swelling itself?

Answer: c

Histamine from mast cells makes the capillaries leaky, so fluid seeps out of the blood into the tissue — that fluid is the swelling. Vasodilation and the extra blood flow give redness and heat (a); prostaglandins add to the pain (b). Inflammation widens vessels; vasoconstriction is the opposite (d).

4Ch. 1313.4 · Antibody classes
  • textbook
detail

A diagram shows an antibody made of two Y-shaped units joined at their stems by a joining piece. Which class is it?

Answer: d

Table 13.4: IgA is the dimer (or monomer) — in tears, saliva, mucus, gut secretions and breast milk, where it stops pathogens attaching to surface linings. IgM is the pentamer — five Ys joined like wheel spokes (a); count the Ys, not the shape of the joining piece. IgG, IgD and IgE are single Ys (monomers).

5Ch. 1313.8 · Allergies
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which statement about anaphylactic shock is false?

Answer: b

In anaphylaxis histamine goes body-wide and widens the vessels and makes them leaky, so blood pools in the capillaries and blood pressure falls — dizziness, sometimes unconsciousness. That is why an EpiPen works: epinephrine constricts the vessels and holds blood pressure up. The rest are true: IgE made at first exposure coats mast cells and basophils; the allergen then triggers histamine release, and effects spread within minutes.

6Ch. 1313.2 · Defensive cells
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A natural killer cell has attached to a virus-infected cell. How does it kill the target?

Answer: b

The NK cell's "kiss of death": proteins that punch pores in the target's membrane; it leaks, cannot hold a constant internal environment, and bursts. Engulfing is phagocytosis — neutrophils and macrophages (a). Histamine comes from mast cells and basophils (c). Activating complement is one of the things antibodies do (d).

7Ch. 1313.4 · Helper T cells
  • textbook
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

HIV infects and destroys helper T cells. Which defenses does the person lose as a result?

Answer: a

The helper T cell is the "on" switch for both branches: it activates B cells (whose plasma cells make antibodies) and cytotoxic T cells. Without it neither branch switches on, so losing only one (b, c) is wrong. White cells are still made in the red marrow (d), and innate defenses such as macrophages and NK cells still work.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

8Ch. 1313.4 · PLAN
  • textbook
  • lab manual

An antibody binds a bacterial toxin so the toxin can no longer harm body cells. Which antibody action is this?

Answer: a

Neutralization — binding toxins or viruses so they cannot do harm. Agglutination (c) clumps cells and precipitation (d) clumps free antigens so they settle out; opsonization (b) coats the antigen so phagocytes can grip it. Engulfing is phagocytosis, and bursting is lysis by complement — neither is neutralization.

9Ch. 1313.9 · Transplant rejection
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A month after a heart transplant, the patient's immune system begins attacking the new heart. Which cells do most of the damage?

Answer: d

The donor's cells carry different MHC self markers, so they are read as nonself, and rejection is a cell-mediated response: cytotoxic (effector) T cells attack transplanted cells, as they do infected and cancer cells. Antibodies mainly target antigens free in body fluids (a). Suppressor T cells switch the response off (b); helper T cells switch it on but do not kill (c).

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

10Ch. 1313.1 · Three lines of defense
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which of these belongs to the third line of defense rather than the first or second?

Answer: d

Cytotoxic T cells are lymphocytes of the adaptive response — the third line: specific, with memory. The second line is innate and nonspecific: phagocytes, eosinophils, NK cells, interferons, complement, inflammation and fever. NK cells kill the same targets as cytotoxic T cells — infected and cancer cells — but without antigen-specific activation, which is the trap.

11Ch. 1313.9 · Autoimmune disorders
  • textbook
detail

Which pairing of disorder and the immune agent that mainly causes it is incorrect?

Answer: d

Organ-specific autoimmune disorders (type 1 diabetes, Hashimoto's) are usually T cells gone awry; non-organ-specific ones such as systemic lupus erythematosus are usually B-cell antibodies. Rheumatic fever is antibodies against strep that also hit the heart valves and joints (molecular mimicry). Anaphylactic shock is driven by IgE antibodies.

12Ch. 1313.2 · Defensive proteins
  • textbook

A cell infected with a virus secretes interferon before it dies. What does the interferon accomplish?

Answer: b

Interferons cannot save the infected cell; they warn the neighbours, which make proteins that block viral replication, and they attract macrophages and NK cells to destroy infected cells — so the virus spreads more slowly. Punching holes is NK cells and complement (a); interferon is a second-line, innate protein, not adaptive (c); redness and swelling come from histamine (d).

13Ch. 1313.2 · Defensive cells
  • textbook

Ch. 13 lists the defensive cells of the second line of defense. Which of these is not one of them?

Answer: b

Table 13.1's defensive cells: phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), eosinophils and NK cells — all innate. The helper T cell is a lymphocyte of the adaptive third line; it switches the specific response on rather than killing anything itself.

14Ch. 1313.5 · Clonal selection
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A student writes: "A naive B cell takes in a new antigen and then shapes an antibody to fit it." What is wrong with this?

Answer: a

Clonal selection: each lymphocyte is already programmed for one antigen before it meets it. The antigen selects the matching B cell, which clones into plasma cells (which mass-produce that antibody) and memory cells. B cells bind antigen directly with their receptors (b, d), and it is plasma cells, not memory cells, that make the antibody (c).

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

15Ch. 1313.2 · Defensive proteins
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which of these is NOT an effect of the complement system?

Answer: b

Complement destroys pathogens (pores, water rushes in, the cell bursts), enhances phagocytosis (attracts phagocytes and coats the microbe) and stimulates inflammation (wider, leakier vessels → redness and swelling). Fever comes from pyrogens, which raise the hypothalamus's set point.

16Ch. 1313.2 Complement
  • textbook

A lab test measures a patient's complement system. What, exactly, is it measuring?

Answer: b

The complement system is at least 20 proteins circulating inactive in the blood until an infection switches them on; then they punch pores in bacteria, enhance inflammation and promote phagocytosis. They are not cells (a) and not antibodies (c) — though the classical pathway is triggered by antibody bound to antigen.

17Ch. 1313.3 Self vs nonself
  • textbook

A transplanted kidney carries no pathogen, yet T cells attack it. What on its cells marks them as nonself?

Answer: d

MHC markers label every body cell as "self"; yours differ from everyone's except an identical twin's. Mature T cells pass by cells with the proper markers and attack cells with foreign ones — the basis of transplant rejection. Interferons are secreted warnings, not markers; B-cell receptors sit on B cells only.

18Ch. 1313.3 Lymphocyte maturation
  • textbook
  • lecture

A child is born without a thymus. Which lymphocytes fail to mature?

Answer: b

T lymphocytes mature in the thymus (the T), where they learn to recognize the body's own MHC markers. B cells are thought to mature in the bone marrow; plasma cells are activated B cells. Sources disagree: Ch. 13 hedges ("it is thought that B cells mature in the bone marrow"), while deck slide 39 states it flatly.

19Ch. 1313.5 Primary vs secondary
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A person meets the same antigen twice, 60 days apart. Compared with the first, the second antibody response is

Answer: a

The primary response is slow — a lag of several days, peaking at 1–2 weeks — because the few matching lymphocytes must be found. The secondary response is faster and stronger because long-lived memory cells are already programmed for the antigen. It is just as specific (d); the speed comes from memory cells, not macrophages (c).

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

20Ch. 1313.6 Active vs passive
  • textbook

A child gets a measles vaccine and, years later, is exposed but does not fall ill. What kind of immunity protected her?

Answer: b

A vaccine exposes the body to a harmless form of the antigen, so her own immune system makes antibodies and memory cells — artificial active immunity, slow to build but lasting. Passive immunity is borrowed, ready-made antibodies (from the placenta, milk or an injection) and fades within weeks to months. Vaccines carry antigen, not antibodies (a, d).

21Ch. 1313.1 Lines of defense
  • textbook

Which pairing of defender and line of defense is correct?

Answer: c

First line — barriers: skin, mucous membranes, their chemicals. Second line — nonspecific innate defenses: phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), NK cells, interferons, complement, inflammation, fever. Third line — the adaptive response: lymphocytes, plasma cells and their antibodies. One Mastering matching item calls neutrophils "a part of the first line"; the book puts them in the second.

22Ch. 1313.2 First line
  • textbook

Tears and saliva carry lysozyme, which breaks down bacterial cell walls. What kind of defense is it?

Answer: a

Lysozyme is an enzyme — a chemical barrier — and it works at the body surface before pathogens get in, so it belongs to the first line. Skin and mucus are the physical barriers of that line. The second line acts once a pathogen has breached the barriers.

23Ch. 1313.2 Interferons
  • textbook

A drug that blocked interferons would most directly weaken which defense?

Answer: b

Interferons are small proteins that virus-infected cells secrete before they die; they warn neighbouring cells to block viral replication. Pore-punching (a) is complement; vessel dilation (c) is histamine from mast cells; raising the set point (d) is pyrogens, causing fever.

24Ch. 1313.4 Helper T cells
  • textbook

Helper T cells activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells. How do they pass that signal on?

Answer: d

An activated helper T cell secretes chemical messengers (cytokines) that call the matching B cells and cytotoxic T cells into action. Displaying pieces of the invader (b) is what antigen-presenting cells do; releasing antibodies (a) is the plasma cells' job; antibiotics are drugs, not body products (c).

25Ch. 1313.5 Eight steps
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Put these four steps of the adaptive immune response in order: Alert, Detection, Alarm, Threat.

Answer: b

Threat (an invader gets past the first line) → Detection (a macrophage finds and engulfs it) → Alert (the macrophage shows its antigen to a helper T cell) → Alarm (the helper T cell switches on both branches). Then building specific defenses, defense, continued surveillance and withdrawal of forces. Lecture and Table 13.3 give eight steps; the study guide's mnemonic TDAABFC stops at seven (no withdrawal).

In lecture: "I want you to know the 8 steps involved in the adaptive immune system" (Mon 11/16); "Know all of the steps. Please. Be familiar with all of the steps." — Wed 11/18

26Ch. 1313.5 Eight steps
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Whalen's guard dog brings him a stranger's wallet from inside his fence. In the eight steps, what does the macrophage do at the step called Alert?

Answer: b

At Alert the macrophage places a piece of the invader — the antigen — on its own MHC marker and shows it to a helper T cell, which it activates. Engulfing and digesting (a) is the step before, Detection. Antibodies come from plasma cells (c), and cloning (d) is what selected lymphocytes do when building specific defenses.

In lecture: "I want you to know the 8 steps involved in the adaptive immune system" (Mon 11/16); "Know all of the steps. Please. Be familiar with all of the steps." — Wed 11/18

27Ch. 1313.5 Eight steps
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

An activated helper T cell switches on naive B cells and naive cytotoxic T cells against one antigen. Which of the eight steps is this?

Answer: d

Alarm — the effector helper T cell activates both lines (antibody-mediated and cell-mediated) against that antigen. Detection is the macrophage engulfing the invader; Alert is the macrophage presenting antigen to the helper T cell; Defense is antibodies and cytotoxic T cells actually eliminating it.

In lecture: "I want you to know the 8 steps involved in the adaptive immune system" (Mon 11/16); "Know all of the steps. Please. Be familiar with all of the steps." — Wed 11/18

28Ch. 1313.5 Eight steps
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

During the step "building specific defenses," what does an activated B cell divide to produce?

Answer: a

Table 13.2: "When activated by helper T cells, the B cell divides to form plasma cells and memory cells." Plasma cells are the antibody factories; memory B cells wait for a repeat exposure. Cytotoxic and memory T cells (b) come from an activated T cell. Deck slides 52–53 file clonal selection under Alarm; Table 13.3 makes it step 5 — the cells produced are the same either way.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

29Ch. 1313.5 Eight steps
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which cells carry out "continued surveillance," the seventh step of the adaptive response?

Answer: c

Memory cells, formed when helper T, cytotoxic T and B cells were activated, stay on patrol — possibly for life — for a swift response if the antigen returns. Plasma cells (a) make antibody during the fight; suppressor T cells (b) end it; macrophages (d) are the detectors at step 2.

In lecture: "I want you to know the 8 steps involved in the adaptive immune system" (Mon 11/16); "Know all of the steps. Please. Be familiar with all of the steps." — Wed 11/18

30Ch. 1313.5 Eight steps
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

The infection is cleared. Which cell carries out the last step, withdrawal of forces, and how?

Answer: a

Step 8: once the antigen is destroyed, suppressor T cells — the "off" switch — suppress the activity of B and T cells. Whalen: the surplus soldiers are made to "commit suicide" and the factories shut down; some memory cells are kept. Helper T cells are the "on" switch (b); memory cells do not kill other cells (c).

In lecture: "I want you to know the 8 steps involved in the adaptive immune system" (Mon 11/16); "Know all of the steps. Please. Be familiar with all of the steps." — Wed 11/18

31Ch. 1313.4 Table 13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Table 13.2 calls one T cell the "on" switch and another the "off" switch for both lines of the immune response. Which pairing is correct?

Answer: d

Helper T — the "on" switch: activates B cells and T cells. Suppressor T — the "off" switch: suppresses B and T cells after the invader is destroyed. Cytotoxic T cells are neither switch; they are the effectors of the cell-mediated response, destroying infected cells and cancer cells.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

32Ch. 1313.4 Table 13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which cell in Table 13.2 is the effector of the antibody-mediated response — the one Whalen called an "antibody factory"?

Answer: c

Plasma cells are activated B cells; they secrete antibodies specific to extracellular antigens such as toxins, bacteria and free viruses — about 1,000 antibodies per second, in lecture ("You might want to write that one down"). Memory B cells (a) wait for the next exposure; helper T (b) switches the response on; cytotoxic T (d) is the effector of the cell-mediated branch.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

33Ch. 1313.4 Table 13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

According to Table 13.2, which cells can give rise to memory cells?

Answer: c

Memory cells are "generated by B cells or any type of T cell during an immune response"; they enable a quick, efficient response on later exposures and may live for years. Macrophages and dendritic cells (d) are antigen-presenting cells, not lymphocytes, and make no memory cells.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

34Ch. 1313.5 Defense
  • lecture
  • textbook

A cytotoxic T cell finds a body cell carrying its antigen. How does it kill that cell?

Answer: d

The effector (cytotoxic) T cell releases perforins, which form holes in cells with that antigen — "not that different than the Mac Attack," the complement membrane attack complex. A cell with a hole in it does not heal; it bursts. Antibodies come from plasma cells (a); engulfing is phagocytosis (b); histamine comes from mast cells and basophils (c).

35Ch. 1313.4 Two branches
  • lecture
  • textbook

A virus is free in the blood on day 1 and has entered body cells by day 3. Which branch of the adaptive response can reach it at each stage?

Answer: a

The antibody-mediated response handles antigens free in body fluids — toxins and extracellular pathogens. Viruses are extracellular "for a time"; once inside cells, antibodies can no longer reach them, and the cell-mediated response takes over: cytotoxic T cells burst the infected cells before they release more virus.

36Ch. 1313.3 Adaptive response
  • lecture
  • textbook

The adaptive response differs from the first and second lines of defense in two key characteristics. Which two?

Answer: a

Specificity — directed at one enemy, recognized by its antigen — and memory — on a second exposure it hits hard and fast. It is the slowest line (at least about three days), not the fastest (b). Inflammation, fever, phagocytosis and complement lysis (c, d) are nonspecific second-line defenses.

37Ch. 1313.3 Self vs nonself
  • lecture

Whalen calls the MHC I molecule a "pass" every body cell must show. In his account, what happens to a cell whose pass the security forces cannot see?

Answer: a

Mon 11/16: every cell should show an MHC I "pass" saying "I belong here" at all times; when the security forces do not see it, they kill the cell — "No questions asked." Foreign invaders never carry the pass. MHC = major histocompatibility complex; there are MHC I and MHC II.

38Ch. 1313.3 Antigens
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which of these would NOT be expected to act as an antigen?

Answer: c

Antigens are things on a cell's surface that can trigger an immune response — usually large molecules: proteins, polysaccharides, nucleic acids, lipoproteins, glycolipids and glycoproteins (lecture's list; Ch. 13 names the first three). A water molecule is far too small and is everywhere in the body. (The lab's glossary calls an antigen a "small piece" of material — the conflict is noted on the Ch. 13 tab.)

39Ch. 1313.3 Lymphocyte maturation
  • lecture
  • textbook

In the thymus, a maturing T cell reacts to the body's own MHC markers as foreign. What happens to it?

Answer: c

The thymus — Whalen's "murder university" — kills T cells that treat self (MHC) markers as foreign; fewer than 5% graduate, and "to fail means to be killed." One that escaped would shoot its own side: an autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis or lupus. T cells form in the bone marrow but mature in the thymus.

40Ch. 1313.5 Clonal selection
  • lecture
  • textbook

Whalen compares finding the right B cell to finding one card in a deck. Why does the first adaptive response take days?

Answer: d

Clonal selection: you already have B cells against antigens you have never met, each with its own receptor; the slow part is finding the right one, then getting it to divide into thousands of clones. Nothing is built to fit the antigen afterwards (a). Memory cells exist only after a first exposure (c).

41Ch. 1313.2 Phagocytes
  • lecture
  • textbook

A macrophage has wrapped a bacterium in a pinched-off piece of its own membrane. What happens next?

Answer: b

Phagocytosis: the cell engulfs the particle in a phagosome, which joins a lysosome full of digestive enzymes that "melt this thing down." The cell saves a piece that identifies the invader — the antigen — and displays it to show other cells. Macrophages come from monocytes that leave the blood.

42Ch. 1313.2 Phagocytes
  • lecture

Phagocytes leave the blood and track down an infection by following interleukins and cytokines released by damaged cells. What is this movement called?

Answer: c

Chemotaxis — movement driven by a chemical trail, weak far away and stronger close up; Whalen's image is finding a sandwich in the room blindfolded, by smell. Phagocytosis (a) is the eating that follows; agglutination (b) is antibody clumping; opsonization (d) is coating an antigen so phagocytes can grip it.

43Ch. 1313.2 Defensive cells
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

A traveller back from abroad has a complete blood count showing eosinophilia. Which cause did Whalen name first?

Answer: a

Eosinophils stain red with eosin and attack pathogens too big for phagocytosis, such as parasitic worms; an eosinophil count that is too high (eosinophilia) points first to a parasite — hence his question about recent travel — and second to a blood cancer (leukemia).

44Ch. 1313.2 Defensive cells
  • lecture
detail

In lecture, which white cell did Whalen say makes histaminase, the enzyme that breaks down histamine?

Answer: c

Lecture only: the eosinophil makes histaminase. Basophils and mast cells (a, b) are the two cells that release histamine. Neither Ch. 13 nor the Lab 12 handout names histaminase; the lab gives eosinophils only "a role in allergies."

45Ch. 1313.2 Defensive cells
  • lecture
  • textbook

Minutes after a splinter, which white cell arrives first at the wound, and how common is it among white cells?

Answer: c

Neutrophils arrive first and are the most numerous white cell — about 7 of every 10 (also called PMNs, polymorphonuclear: "nucleus of many shapes"). Monocytes arrive second and quickly become macrophages (a).

46Ch. 1313.2 Complement
  • lecture
  • textbook

Why does a bacterium burst once complement proteins have formed a membrane attack complex in its membrane?

Answer: d

The membrane attack complex (MAC) is a hole the cell cannot close, so it can no longer regulate water; water rushes in until it bursts (lysis) — Whalen's water balloon left on a faucet. Complement also enhances phagocytosis and stimulates inflammation.

47Ch. 1313.2 Inflammation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Whalen compares inflammation to flooding a battlefield into a mud pit. What main purpose does he give it?

Answer: a

Inflammation slows the spread of infection and keeps it localized — "I want to keep it localized to this village right here" — while the wider, leakier vessels bring in defensive cells: neutrophils first, then monocytes that become macrophages. Raising the set point (d) is the job of pyrogens.

48Ch. 1313.2 Inflammation
  • lecture
  • textbook

Whalen said mast cells are one of two cells that make and release histamine. Which is the other?

Answer: c

Lecture and Ch. 13 agree: mast cells and basophils (basophils are granulocytic leukocytes). Histamine dilates local vessels and makes them leaky. The eosinophil (a) makes histaminase, which breaks histamine down. Sources differ: the Lab 12 handout says "mast cells and macrophages release histamine", and deck slide 25 names only mast cells.

49Ch. 1313.2 Inflammation
  • lecture
  • textbook

According to lecture, what produces the pain of inflammation?

Answer: b

Wider vessels give redness and heat; leaky vessels give swelling; swelling stretches the tissue, stimulating free nerve endings (nociceptors) — "you interpret that as ouch." Bacterial toxins and prostaglandins also stimulate them. (The lab names bradykinins as its pain chemical.)

50Ch. 1313.2 Fever
  • lecture
  • textbook

Pyrogens cause a fever by resetting the body's thermostat. Where is that thermostat?

Answer: d

Pyrogens reset the hypothalamus — the brain's thermostat — to a higher temperature. The thalamus (b) is a relay station next to it; the thyroid (a) sets metabolic rate, not the set point.

51Ch. 1313.2 Fever
  • lecture
  • textbook

Why does a mild to moderate fever help the body fight a bacterial infection, according to Whalen?

Answer: c

Whalen: the bacteria "do not give a shit about" 40–41 °C — the heat does nothing to them (a); what it does is let immune cells work better and faster, like warming up before a match. Ch. 13 agrees on the faster defenses and adds a second benefit: the liver and spleen pull iron from the blood, which many bacteria need. Over 105 °F (40.6 °C) a fever is dangerous and can damage the nervous system.

52Ch. 1313.5 Memory
  • lecture
detail

Whalen had chickenpox at 11. If his last memory cells against varicella zoster die and he meets the virus again in his 60s, what does he expect?

Answer: a

Memory cells keep up continued surveillance, possibly for life; if the last one dies before "training a replacement," immunity is lost. Meeting varicella zoster again later in life brings shingles, not chickenpox. Smallpox (c) is a different, eradicated virus. Antibodies themselves do not last for life (d) — memory cells are what persist.

53Ch. 1313.5 Primary vs secondary
  • lecture
  • textbook

Why do most vaccines come as two or three doses rather than one?

Answer: d

The first exposure gives a primary response: antibody titers (concentration in the blood) rise slowly and not very high. A later dose meets memory cells and gives a secondary response — titers rise much faster and much higher. Vaccines carry antigen, not antibodies (a).

54Ch. 1313.6 Active vs passive
  • lecture
  • textbook

According to lecture, a newborn's first protection comes from colostrum. What kind of immunity is it, and how long does Whalen say it lasts?

Answer: c

Colostrum — what the mammary glands make for the first ~3 days — is loaded with antibodies: passive immunity, borrowed rather than made, so it is short-lived — about 6 months in lecture (both days). Sources differ: Ch. 13 §13.6 says maternal antibodies from the placenta last up to 3 months; on a book question, use that. The 3 days (d) is how long colostrum is made, not how long it protects.

55Ch. 1313.7 Monoclonal antibodies
  • lecture
  • textbook

A home pregnancy test detects human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) in urine. What does the test use to detect it?

Answer: c

Monoclonal antibodies — a group of identical antibodies that bind one specific antigen — used in research, clinical diagnosis and treatment; deck slide 73's example is antibodies to hCG in pregnancy tests. A mixture from many plasma cells (d) would bind many antigens. Whalen called hCG "this antibody" — it is a hormone; the antibodies are against it.

56Ch. 1313.8 Autoimmune disorders
  • lecture
  • textbook

In type 1 diabetes, which cells does the immune system destroy?

Answer: d

An organ-specific autoimmune disorder: T cells kill the insulin-making beta cells in the islets of Langerhans of the pancreas, usually in fetal development or early childhood, so the person must take insulin for life. The thyroid (b) is the target in Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Whalen's other organ-specific example.

57Ch. 1313.8 Allergies
  • lecture
  • textbook

On first exposure to peanut protein, what does a person who becomes allergic make, and where does it go?

Answer: d

First exposure: the allergen makes plasma cells release IgE, which binds to mast cells or basophils. Later exposure: the allergen combines with that IgE and the cells release histamine — dilated, leaky vessels: redness, heat, swelling, pain. Histamine comes from mast cells and basophils, not plasma cells (b).

58Ch. 1313.8 Allergies
  • lecture
  • textbook

Why is epinephrine, given by an EpiPen, the emergency treatment for anaphylactic shock?

Answer: a

In anaphylaxis histamine goes body-wide: vessels dilate and leak, blood pressure falls, and airway swelling makes breathing hard. Epinephrine constricts the blood vessels and prevents the blood-pressure drop. Dilating vessels (d) is what histamine already did. Antihistamines block histamine in ordinary allergies; common anaphylaxis triggers are bee and wasp stings, penicillin and foods.

59Ch. 1313.2 First line
  • lecture
detail

Why are urinary tract infections more common in females, as Whalen explained it?

Answer: b

Bacteria have much less distance to travel to the bladder: the female urethra is about 4 cm, the male about 20 cm. Urine is a first-line defense because it is acidic (about pH 6), should be sterile, and flushes the urethra each time. (Ch. 16 says the short urethra "perhaps" explains it; Whalen gives it as the one reason.)

60Ch. 1313.2 First line
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Which statement about intact skin as a first-line barrier matches lecture?

Answer: a

The stratum corneum is 15–30 layers of dead keratinocytes — water-resistant, not waterproof; submerged for about two days, it starts to fall apart. It resists most toxins and enzymes. Sweat (salty) and sebum (lipid-rich) add chemical protection. Skin and mucous membranes are the first line (d).

61Ch. 1313.1 Cancer
  • lecture
  • textbook

Whalen described a cancer cell as one that has lost contact inhibition. What does that mean?

Answer: c

Normal cells stop dividing when they touch their neighbours — contact inhibition (a describes the normal cell). After mutations, a cancer cell loses it and divides unregulated even with no room left. Cancer cells are among the targets of NK cells and cytotoxic T cells.

62Ch. 1313.5 PLAN
  • lecture
  • textbook

Whalen likened an antigen–antibody complex to a strobe light and siren stuck on the enemy. Which antibody action is that?

Answer: d

PLAN — the deck's four antibody actions: Precipitation (clumping so antigens fall out of circulation; agglutination in blood typing), Lysis with complement, Attraction of phagocytes, Neutralization. The flagged complex makes the enemy easy for phagocytes to find, raising the likelihood of phagocytosis — the action the lab and Ch. 13 call opsonization.

63Ch. 1313.5 Antibody classes
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Whalen said each antibody class's job is Bio 22 material, but Bio 5 teaches their structures. How many antigen-binding sites do a monomer, a dimer and a pentamer have?

Answer: c

A monomer is one Y with 2 binding sites (IgG, IgD, IgE); a dimer two Ys, 4 (IgA); a pentamer five Ys, 10 (IgM) — "a very powerful agglutinating agent." Each arm of a Y binds one antigen, so 1-2-5 (a) counts Ys, not sites.

1Ch. 13short answer13.5 Eight steps
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

List and describe the eight steps of the adaptive immune response.

Model answer

(1) Threat — an invader gets past the first line (skin, mucous membranes). (2) Detection — a macrophage finds it, engulfs it and breaks it down. (3) Alert — the macrophage places a piece of it (the antigen) on its own MHC marker and presents it to a helper T cell, activating it. (4) Alarm — the helper T cell activates both lines: naive B cells and naive cytotoxic T cells. (5) Building specific defenses — clonal selection: the matching B cell divides into plasma cells and memory B cells; the matching T cell into cytotoxic T cells and memory T cells. (6) Defense — antibodies eliminate the antigen (antibody-mediated); cytotoxic T cells burst cells carrying it (cell-mediated). (7) Continued surveillance — memory cells stay for a fast response if it returns. (8) Withdrawal of forces — once it is destroyed, suppressor T cells shut the response down.

One mark per step, named and in order, with the cell that does it. Lecture and Table 13.3 give eight; the guide's mnemonic TDAABFC stops at seven — write all eight. The deck puts clonal selection under Alarm (slides 52–53); naming it at step 5, as the book does, is safe.

In lecture: "I want you to know the 8 steps involved in the adaptive immune system" (Mon 11/16); "Know all of the steps. Please. Be familiar with all of the steps." — Wed 11/18

2Ch. 13short answer13.5 Clonal selection
  • lecture
  • textbook

Describe clonal selection, and use it to explain why a second exposure to an antigen gives a faster, stronger response than the first.

Model answer

Each lymphocyte is already programmed with receptors for one antigen before it ever meets it. When an antigen enters, it binds and so selects the few B or T cells whose receptors fit; those cells divide into a clone of identical cells — effector cells (plasma cells or cytotoxic T cells) and memory cells. In the primary response the few matching cells must first be found and cloned, so antibody titers rise slowly and stay low. The memory cells left behind mean that on a secondary exposure many cells are already programmed for that antigen, so titers rise much faster and higher — the basis of vaccine boosters.

Marks for: receptors exist before exposure; the antigen selects the matching cell; it clones into effector and memory cells; memory cells explain the faster, higher secondary response.

3Ch. 13short answer13.8 Allergies
  • lecture
  • textbook

Describe the steps of an allergic reaction, and explain how antihistamines and epinephrine each treat it.

Model answer

An allergy is an overreaction to an antigen that is harmless to most people (an allergen). First exposure: plasma cells make IgE antibodies, which attach to mast cells and basophils. Later exposure: the allergen binds that IgE and the cells release histamine, which dilates vessels and makes them leaky — redness, heat, swelling and pain. Antihistamines block histamine's effects. In anaphylactic shock the reaction goes body-wide: vessels dilate, blood pressure falls, breathing is hard; epinephrine (an EpiPen) constricts the blood vessels and holds blood pressure up.

Marks for IgE on mast cells/basophils at first exposure, histamine release at the next, histamine's effects, and the two treatments with how each works.

1Ch. 13flashcard13.7 Autoimmune disorders
  • textbook

Autoimmune disorder

Back

The immune system fails to tell self from nonself and attacks the body's own tissues — "friendly fire."

2Ch. 13flashcard13.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Pathogens — the six types

Back

Disease-causing bacteria, viruses, protozoans, fungi, parasitic worms and prions.

3Ch. 13flashcard13.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

The three lines of defense

Back

First — nonspecific surface barriers (skin, mucous membranes, their chemicals). Second — nonspecific internal defenses (phagocytes, NK cells, interferons, complement, inflammation, fever). Third — the adaptive response: specific, with memory, at least ~3 days to start.

4Ch. 13flashcard13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Phagocytes

Back

Cells that engulf and digest invaders (phagocytosis) — neutrophils (arrive first, ~7 in 10 WBCs) and macrophages. They find the site by chemotaxis.

5Ch. 13flashcard13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Macrophages

Back

"Large eaters" — monocytes that have left the blood. Engulf invaders in a phagosome, digest them with a lysosome, and present the antigen to helper T cells (e.g. alveolar macrophages in the lungs).

6Ch. 13flashcard13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Natural killer (NK) cells

Back

White cells that search out abnormal cells — cancer cells and virus-infected cells — and kill them by punching pores in their membrane, not by engulfing.

7Ch. 13flashcard13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Interferon

Back

Small proteins released by a virus-infected cell before it dies: they attract macrophages and NK cells and make neighbouring cells produce proteins that block viral replication.

8Ch. 13flashcard13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Complement — three things it does

Back

A set of blood proteins that (1) destroy pathogens — the membrane attack complex holes them and they burst; (2) enhance phagocytosis; (3) stimulate inflammation.

9Ch. 13flashcard13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Inflammatory response — the four signs

Back

Redness, heat, swelling, pain. Purpose: keep the infection local and slow its spread while defensive cells arrive.

10Ch. 13flashcard13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Redness (in inflammation)

Back

Histamine dilates local vessels → more blood flow → redness and heat. Leaky vessels → swelling; swelling stretches tissue → pain.

11Ch. 13flashcard13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Histamine

Back

The chemical released by mast cells and basophils that dilates local vessels and makes them leaky. Blocked by antihistamines; broken down by eosinophils' histaminase (lecture).

12Ch. 13flashcard13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Mast cells

Back

Tissue cells that release histamine in inflammation; in an allergy their surface is coated with IgE from the first exposure.

13Ch. 13flashcard13.2
  • lecture
  • textbook

Pyrogens

Back

Fever-causing chemicals that reset the hypothalamus (the brain's thermostat) higher. A mild fever lets immune cells work faster; over 105 °F it can damage the nervous system.

14Ch. 13flashcard13.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Adaptive immune response

Back

The third line — directed at one specific antigen and remembering it, so a second exposure is met hard and fast. Carried out by B and T lymphocytes.

15Ch. 13flashcard13.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

MHC markers

Back

Major histocompatibility complex molecules — the self "pass" on your cells saying "I belong here." A macrophage shows antigen on its MHC marker to the helper T cell.

16Ch. 13flashcard13.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Antigen

Back

A molecule, usually large (protein, polysaccharide, nucleic acid, lipoprotein, glycolipid, glycoprotein), that triggers an immune response.

17Ch. 13flashcard13.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

B lymphocytes — where made, where matured

Back

Form and mature in the bone marrow. Become plasma cells (antibody factories) or memory B cells.

18Ch. 13flashcard13.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

T lymphocytes — where made, where matured

Back

Form in the bone marrow, mature in the thymus, where any that attack self (MHC) markers are killed. They fight cell to cell.

19Ch. 13flashcard13.3
  • lecture
  • textbook

Effector cells

Back

Activated lymphocytes that attack the invader now — plasma cells and cytotoxic T cells. They live only days.

20Ch. 13flashcard13.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Memory cells

Back

Made by B cells or any type of T cell; they do not fight but remember the antigen, giving a quick, strong response on later exposure. May live for years.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

21Ch. 13flashcard13.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Antibody-mediated immune response

Back

Against antigens free in body fluids — toxins, bacteria, free viruses. Plasma cells secrete antibodies that bind and help eliminate them.

22Ch. 13flashcard13.4
  • lecture
  • textbook

Cell-mediated immune response

Back

Against cells — virus-infected cells, cancer cells, transplanted cells. Cytotoxic T cells make them burst.

23Ch. 13flashcard13.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Antigen-presenting cell

Back

A macrophage (main), dendritic cell or B cell that engulfs an invader, puts its antigen on its MHC marker and presents it to a helper T cell.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

24Ch. 13flashcard13.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Helper T-cell

Back

The "on" switch for both lines: activated by an APC, it activates B cells and cytotoxic T cells.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

25Ch. 13flashcard13.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Cytotoxic T cell

Back

Effector of the cell-mediated response: destroys infected body cells and cancer cells, using perforins.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

26Ch. 13flashcard13.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Suppressor T-cell

Back

The "off" switch: suppresses B and T cells once the invader is destroyed — step 8, withdrawal of forces.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

27Ch. 13flashcard13.4
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Plasma cells

Back

Activated B cells — the antibody factories (about 1,000 antibodies a second, in lecture), the effectors of the antibody-mediated response.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend... you understand and know this table." — Table 13.2, the cells of the adaptive response, Wed 11/18

28Ch. 13flashcard13.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

The eight steps of the adaptive response

Back

Threat → Detection → Alert → Alarm → Building specific defenses (clonal selection) → Defense → Continued surveillance → Withdrawal of forces. (Guide mnemonic TDAABFC covers the first seven.)

In lecture: "I want you to know the 8 steps involved in the adaptive immune system" (Mon 11/16); "Know all of the steps. Please. Be familiar with all of the steps." — Wed 11/18

29Ch. 13flashcard13.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Clonal selection

Back

The antigen selects the few lymphocytes whose receptors already fit it; each divides into a clone of effector and memory cells.

30Ch. 13flashcard13.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Antibodies

Back

Y-shaped proteins (immunoglobulins) secreted by plasma cells, each binding one specific antigen.

31Ch. 13flashcard13.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

PLAN — what antibodies do

Back

Precipitation, Lysis (with complement), Attraction of phagocytes, Neutralization.

32Ch. 13flashcard13.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Precipitation

Back

Antibodies link antigens into clumps too big to move, which fall out of circulation. Clumping of cells, as in blood typing, is agglutination.

33Ch. 13flashcard13.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Lysis

Back

Bursting of a cell — with complement, whose membrane attack complex lets water flood in.

34Ch. 13flashcard13.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Neutralization

Back

Antibodies bind a toxin or virus so it can no longer do what it was doing.

35Ch. 13flashcard13.5
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Immunoglobulins — the five classes

Back

IgG (crosses placenta, longest-lived), IgM (acute response; pentamer, 10 sites), IgE (parasites and allergies), IgA (mucus and secretions; dimer, 4 sites), IgD (membrane-bound only). Monomer = 2 sites. Lecture: know the structures; jobs in depth are Bio 22.

36Ch. 13flashcard13.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Perforins

Back

Proteins released by cytotoxic T cells (and NK cells) that hole the target cell's membrane so it bursts.

37Ch. 13flashcard13.5
  • lecture
  • textbook

Antibody titer

Back

The antibody concentration in the blood. Primary response: rises slowly, stays low. Secondary: rises fast and high.

38Ch. 13flashcard13.6
  • lecture
  • textbook

Active immunity — natural and artificial

Back

Your body makes its own memory B and T cells after meeting the antigen. Natural: infection. Artificial: vaccination (a harmless form of the antigen). Long-lived.

39Ch. 13flashcard13.6
  • lecture
  • textbook

Passive immunity — natural and artificial

Back

Ready-made antibodies from another person or animal; no memory cells, short-lived. Natural: placenta, breast milk, colostrum. Artificial: injected antibodies (e.g. gamma globulin, antitoxins).

40Ch. 13flashcard13.7
  • lecture
  • textbook

Monoclonal antibodies

Back

A group of identical antibodies that bind one specific antigen; used in research, diagnosis (home pregnancy tests detect hCG) and treatment.

41Ch. 13flashcard13.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

Three autoimmune disorders

Back

Type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus (also Hashimoto's thyroiditis, multiple sclerosis). Organ-specific ones are usually T cells; body-wide ones (lupus) usually B cells.

42Ch. 13flashcard13.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

Allergy and allergen

Back

An overreaction of the immune system to an antigen harmless to most people — the allergen (pollen, dust mites, peanuts, bee stings).

43Ch. 13flashcard13.8
  • lecture
  • textbook

Anaphylactic shock — and its treatment

Back

The most extreme allergic reaction: body-wide histamine, vessels dilate, blood pressure falls, breathing is hard. Treated with epinephrine (EpiPen), which constricts vessels.

Ch. 13a — Special Topic — Infectious Disease

Week 14 · study page · 28 multiple choice · 3 short answer · 20 flashcards

1Ch. 13a13a.1 Fungi
  • textbook

A wrestler develops an itchy, ring-shaped skin rash called ringworm. What causes it?

Answer: c

Despite the name, ringworm is a fungal skin infection, listed in Ch. 13a with athlete's foot. Fungi secrete digestive enzymes and absorb the nutrients — in or on a human, digesting body cells. The "worm" in the name is the trap (b).

2Ch. 13a13a.1 Pathogens
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which list contains only types of pathogen, as named in lecture and the book?

Answer: a

The six pathogen types are bacteria, viruses, protozoans, fungi, parasitic worms and prions — Whalen's list on Mon 11/16 and §13a.1. An allergen (b) is a harmless antigen the body overreacts to; an antigen (c) is a molecule that triggers a response, carried by pathogens and your own cells alike; a toxin (d) is something a bacterium makes, not a pathogen itself.

3Ch. 13a13a.1 Virulence
  • textbook

The typhoid bacterium causes disease every time it infects someone; the yeast Candida albicans only sometimes does. Which property of the two pathogens differs?

Answer: c

Virulence is a pathogen's relative ability to cause disease — how easily it invades tissue and how much damage it does. Typhoid is the book's highly virulent example, Candida its moderately virulent one. A vector (a) is an animal that carries a disease between hosts; antigens (b) are what the immune system recognises; a capsid (d) is a virus's protein coat, and neither of these is a virus.

4Ch. 13a13a.1 Bacteria
  • textbook

A bacterium and a protozoan are both single cells. Which statement correctly separates them?

Answer: b

Bacteria are prokaryotes — no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Protozoans are eukaryotes with a well-defined nucleus, like our own cells. Both have DNA (a) and a plasma membrane (c), and both include pathogens (d) — malaria and giardiasis are protozoan diseases.

5Ch. 13a13a.1 Bacteria
  • textbook

A lab report describes the bacteria in a sample as rod-shaped and usually single. Which shape term fits?

Answer: d

The cell wall sets three shapes: bacillus — a rod, usually single; coccus — a sphere, single, in pairs or in chains (a); spirillum — a spiral or corkscrew (b). A capsid (c) is a virus's protein coat, not a bacterial shape.

6Ch. 13a13a.1 Bacteria
  • textbook

A bacterium copies its DNA, then pinches in half so each new cell has a full copy. What is this process called?

Answer: a

Binary fission is how bacteria reproduce — some every 20 minutes, so one cell could in theory become trillions in a day. Mitosis (d) is division of a eukaryotic nucleus; bacteria have none. Budding (b) is how some viruses leave a host cell, and lysis (c) is a host cell bursting.

7Ch. 13a13a.1 Virulence factors
  • textbook

Two strains of the same bacterium differ in one structure. Phagocytes engulf strain A easily but cannot engulf strain B. What does strain B most likely have?

Answer: c

A capsule lets bacteria stick to surfaces and stops phagocytes engulfing them. Flagella (a) let bacteria move and spread through tissue; pili (b) attach them to target cells. All bacteria have ribosomes (d) — they are where antibiotics that block protein synthesis act.

8Ch. 13a13a.1 Toxins
  • textbook
detail

A family eats improperly home-canned green beans and one member later dies of botulism. How does the botulism toxin kill?

Answer: d

The Clostridium botulinum toxin — one of the most toxic substances known — interferes with nerves, especially motor nerves, and kills by paralysing the breathing muscles. Kidney failure (a) is the danger from one E. coli toxin in children and the elderly. Bursting red blood cells (b) and dissolving what holds muscle together (c) are the two enzymes of gas gangrene, another Clostridium.

9Ch. 13a13a.1 Antibiotics
  • textbook

One class of antibiotic blocks the synthesis of the bacterial cell wall. Why does it harm the bacteria but not the patient's cells?

Answer: a

Without a wall the bacteria burst, and our cells have no walls to lose. The ribosome difference (b) is real but is the reason the other class — antibiotics that block bacterial protein synthesis — spares us. Division speed (c) and membranes (d) are not how the book explains it.

10Ch. 13a13a.1 Antibiotic resistance
  • textbook

A patient feels better after three days and stops a ten-day course of antibiotics. Why does that make resistance more likely?

Answer: c

Each exposure kills the susceptible bacteria first and leaves the more resistant ones; stopping early may leave exactly those alive to multiply, and repeated exposure strengthens them. The drug does not cause the change (a) — it selects what is already there. Antibodies are made against antigens on pathogens, not against the drug (b).

11Ch. 13a13a.1 Viral replication
  • textbook
  • lecture

Put the steps of viral replication in order.

Answer: d

Figure 13a.2: attachment (surface molecules fit a host receptor) → penetration (the virus enters and loses its capsid) → production of viral nucleic acid and proteins by the host's machinery → assembly of new viruses → release, by budding or by bursting the cell. Assembly cannot come before the parts are made (a); a virus must attach before it can get in (b).

12Ch. 13a13a.1 Viral replication
  • textbook

Cold viruses infect only cells of the respiratory tract, and hepatitis viruses only liver cells. What explains this specificity?

Answer: a

In attachment, the virus's surface molecules (glycoproteins or capsid) must fit a receptor on the host cell, so a virus can infect only cells that bear that receptor. The same rule explains a virus "jumping species" (§13a.3): a mutation that changes the surface molecule lets it fit a new receptor.

13Ch. 13a13a.1 Viral replication
  • lecture

In lecture, Whalen described an RNA virus that carries reverse transcriptase. What does that enzyme do inside the host cell?

Answer: b

Reverse transcriptase makes complementary DNA (cDNA) from the virus's RNA — the reverse of transcription — and the cDNA is inserted into your genome. The cell then transcribes and translates it, making capsid proteins that self-assemble into new virions. Making RNA from DNA (c) is ordinary transcription, done by the host.

14Ch. 13a13a.1 Viral infections
  • textbook

A virus releases new copies slowly, so the infected cell stays alive and keeps producing virus for a long time. What kind of infection is this?

Answer: c

Table 13a.1: persistent — slow release keeps the cell alive and producing virus for a long time. Lytic (a) — rapid release bursts and kills the cell. Latent (b) — the virus sits in the cell without harming it, then starts replicating later. Transformation (d) — viral genes make the cell cancerous.

15Ch. 13a13a.1 Viral infections
  • textbook

After a cold sore heals, herpes simplex can return to blister the same spot months later, often during stress. Where has the virus been in between?

Answer: a

Herpes simplex is the book's example of all three infection types: rapid shedding kills mouth epithelial cells (the blister, b — that is the lytic phase, not the hiding place); slow shedding may show no signs yet still spread it (persistent); then it lies latent in nerve cells, and stress reactivates it to follow the nerve back to the same patch of skin.

16Ch. 13a13a.1 Viruses and cancer
  • textbook

According to Ch. 13a, how can some viruses turn a host cell cancerous?

Answer: b

Some viruses insert their genetic material into a host chromosome near a gene that regulates cell division and alter it; others bring oncogenes (cancer-causing genes) with them (Table 13a.1). Bursting the cell (a) kills it — a dead cell cannot become a tumour.

17Ch. 13a13a.1 Viruses and cancer
  • lecture
detail

As Whalen described it in lecture, which types of human papillomavirus does the HPV vaccine protect against?

Answer: d

Wed 11/18: three subtypes — two with the highest correlation with cervical cancer and one that causes genital warts, given at about 11–12 to girls and boys. With hundreds of HPV types it is "a vest that stops only three kinds of bullet" (b is the trap). HPV is the lecture's example of a virus linked to cancer; Ch. 13a names none. These are his figures — no course source ingested yet checks them.

18Ch. 13a13a.1 Protozoans
  • textbook
detail

A hiker drinks from a clear, pristine-looking mountain stream and has diarrhea for weeks afterwards. Which pathogen is the most likely cause?

Answer: d

Giardiasis — diarrhea lasting weeks, mostly from water contaminated with human or animal feces; even clear wilderness lakes and streams can carry Giardia. Protozoans cause disease with toxins or enzymes that stop host cells working. Legionella (c) lives in air-conditioner cooling water and is inhaled; Ascaris (a) eggs come in contaminated food or drink and the larvae migrate to the lungs.

19Ch. 13a13a.1 Fungi
  • textbook

How do fungi cause disease in a human host?

Answer: b

Fungi infiltrate other organisms, secrete digestive enzymes and absorb the nutrients — in or on a human, digesting body cells: serious lung infections (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis) and milder skin ones (athlete's foot, ringworm). Inserting genes (a) is how some viruses cause cancer; misfolding proteins (c) is the prion; binary fission (d) is bacterial reproduction.

20Ch. 13a13a.1 Parasitic worms
  • textbook

Children in a region with poor sanitation carry Ascaris roundworms. Which is one of the ways the book says parasitic worms make their host ill?

Answer: a

Parasitic worms — flukes, tapeworms, roundworms — harm but usually do not kill the host by releasing toxins into the blood, feeding on blood, or competing with the host for food. In ascariasis that means malnutrition and lung damage, and in large numbers a blocked or perforated intestine. Gene insertion (c) is viral; misfolded brain proteins (d) are prions.

21Ch. 13a13a.1 Prions
  • textbook

A patient is diagnosed with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Which statement about the infectious agent is correct?

Answer: c

CJD is caused by a prion — a misfolded version of a harmless protein normally on nerve cell surfaces, which makes the host's own protein take the abnormal shape. The clumps leave spongelike holes in the brain (a TSE). Prions are not destroyed by heat, UV light or most chemicals (b), and there is no treatment.

22Ch. 13a13a.2 Spread of disease
  • textbook

A student catches a cold after touching a doorknob a sneezing classmate had just used, then rubbing her eyes. How was the virus spread?

Answer: b

Indirect contact — transfer without touching the infected person: pathogen-laden droplets from coughs and sneezes are inhaled or land on surfaces such as doorknobs and are picked up by touch (droplet infection). Most respiratory infections, including the cold, spread this way. Direct contact (a) means touching the infected person — hugging, kissing, sex.

23Ch. 13a13a.2 Vectors
  • textbook
detail

Which pairing of disease and vector is correct?

Answer: c

West Nile virus is spread by mosquitoes, between wild birds and from birds to humans and domestic animals. Lyme disease is a bacterium carried by the deer tick — the most common vector-borne disease in the US. A vector is an animal that carries a disease from one host to another.

24Ch. 13a13a.3 Epidemiology
  • textbook

Which description fits a pandemic?

Answer: d

The four patterns of epidemiology: sporadic — occasional, unpredictable, a few people in a restricted area (a); endemic — always present and of little threat, like the common cold (b); epidemic — sudden and spreading rapidly to many, like smallpox and cholera outbreaks (c); pandemic — a global outbreak, like HIV/AIDS.

25Ch. 13a13a.3 Emerging and reemerging
  • textbook

Tuberculosis had been declining, but cases are rising again because of new drug-resistant strains. How is TB classified?

Answer: a

A reemerging disease reappears after a decline — the book's example is TB, back because of drug-resistant strains (XDR TB is nearly impossible to treat). An emerging disease (b) is one with clinically distinct symptoms whose incidence has been rising, such as HIV, SARS and H1N1 influenza.

26Ch. 13a13a.3 Emerging and reemerging
  • textbook

Which is NOT one of the four factors the book gives for the emergence or reemergence of disease?

Answer: c

The four factors: new or drug-resistant organisms, environmental change (shifting rainfall and temperature, global warming), population growth (more contact with animals that carry pathogens, crowding, air travel) and failure to vaccinate (measles returning to the US in 2015). Better water treatment lowers disease — drinking water is tested for coliform bacteria for exactly that reason.

27Ch. 13a13a.1 Viruses
  • lecture
  • textbook

In lecture, Whalen said many scientists do not consider viruses to be alive. What reason did he give?

Answer: a

A virus cannot replicate by itself: it must get into a cell and convince it to transcribe and translate the viral genes, making capsid proteins that self-assemble into new virions until the cell bursts. Many viruses have only "a handful of genes," coding for their own parts. Some viruses carry DNA, not RNA (b), and antibiotics do not work on viruses (d).

28Ch. 13a13a.3 Epidemiology
  • lecture
detail

According to Whalen, what is the status of smallpox today?

Answer: c

Smallpox is eradicated; samples are kept in only two labs — the CDC in Atlanta and one in Russia. Its mortality is about 33%, and in the US only people born before 1977, born abroad, or who have served in the military are vaccinated. Ch. 13a uses smallpox outbreaks as an example of an epidemic.

1Ch. 13ashort answer13a.1 Viral replication
  • textbook
  • lecture

List and describe the general steps of viral replication, and explain why antibiotics cannot treat a viral infection.

Model answer

(1) Attachment — the virus's surface glycoproteins or capsid fit a receptor on the host cell, which is why a virus infects only certain cells. (2) Penetration — the virus enters and loses its capsid, leaving its DNA or RNA. (3) Production — viral genes direct the host's machinery to copy the viral nucleic acid and make viral coat proteins and enzymes (an RNA virus may first use reverse transcriptase to make DNA that is inserted into the host genome). (4) Assembly of new viruses from those parts. (5) Release — budding through the membrane, which can leave the cell alive, or bursting it, which kills it. Antibiotics block bacterial cell-wall synthesis or bacterial ribosomes; a virus has neither — it uses the host cell's machinery — so there is nothing for the drug to hit.

One mark per step in order, one for the antibiotic point. Source note: Whalen's Wed 11/18 aside has the virus releasing its DNA or RNA into the cell and replicating until the cell bursts; the book has the whole virus enter and allows release by budding without killing the cell. They do not truly conflict — lecture describes the lytic case — but for the book's question, name both kinds of release. Reverse transcriptase is lecture only.

2Ch. 13ashort answer13a.1 Antibiotic resistance
  • textbook

Explain how antibiotic resistance occurs, and give three ways people's use of antibiotics speeds it up.

Model answer

Each exposure to an antibiotic kills the susceptible bacteria first; the more resistant survive and multiply, and repeated exposure strengthens them. The drug also kills beneficial bacteria that kept harmful strains in check. Ways it is sped up: overuse — antibiotics prescribed for colds and flu, which are viral and unaffected; misuse — stopping the course when you feel better, leaving the hardiest bacteria alive; heavy use in hospitals, where most resistant infections such as MRSA arise; and use in agriculture — over 40% of US antibiotics go to livestock, and resistant bacteria can pass to humans.

Marks for the selection mechanism (resistant survivors multiply) and for any three of overuse, misuse, hospitals and agriculture. Saying the antibiotic "causes" the bacteria to mutate loses the first mark.

3Ch. 13ashort answer13a.3 Emerging and reemerging
  • textbook

Describe the four factors that play a role in the emergence or reemergence of a disease, with an example of each.

Model answer

(1) New or drug-resistant organisms — mutation lets a pathogen jump species, or genes of an animal and a human virus mix in one cell (antigenic shift: H1N1 swine flu); improper treatment produced drug-resistant TB. (2) Environmental change — shifts in rainfall and temperature, and global warming, change where pathogens can live. (3) Population growth — suburbs push people into contact with animals that carry pathogens and remove predators (more tick-carrying mice, more Lyme disease); crowded cities and air travel spread disease fast and far. (4) Failure to vaccinate — measles, declared eliminated in the US in 2000, returned in 2015 among unvaccinated children.

One mark per factor with a matching example. The 2015 measles count differs between chapters — 166 people in 19 states in §13a.3, 164 cases in §13.6 — so leave the number out.

1Ch. 13aflashcard13a.1
  • lecture
  • textbook

Pathogens — the six types

Back

Disease-causing bacteria, viruses, protozoans, fungi, parasitic worms and prions.

2Ch. 13aflashcard13a.1
  • textbook

Virulence

Back

A pathogen's relative ability to cause disease — how easily it invades tissue and how much damage it does. Typhoid: high; Candida albicans: moderate.

3Ch. 13aflashcard13a.1
  • textbook

Bacteria

Back

Prokaryotes — no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles, a peptidoglycan cell wall; shaped as cocci, bacilli or spirilla; reproduce by binary fission; harm mostly with toxins and enzymes.

4Ch. 13aflashcard13a.1
  • textbook

Three bacterial virulence factors

Back

Flagella (move and spread through tissue), pili (attach to target cells), capsule (stick to surfaces and resist phagocytes).

5Ch. 13aflashcard13a.1
  • textbook

Two ways antibiotics kill bacteria and spare us

Back

Block cell-wall synthesis (our cells have no walls) or block bacterial protein synthesis (bacterial ribosomes differ slightly from ours).

6Ch. 13aflashcard13a.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Virus

Back

DNA or RNA in a protein coat (capsid), sometimes inside an envelope with glycoproteins. Replicates only inside a host cell using its machinery, so most biologists do not consider it alive.

7Ch. 13aflashcard13a.1
  • textbook

Latent infection — and an example

Back

The virus sits in the cell without harming it, then starts replicating later and kills cells. Herpes simplex, latent in nerve cells, reactivated by stress.

8Ch. 13aflashcard13a.1
  • textbook

Persistent infection — and an example

Back

Slow release of new viruses keeps the cell alive and producing virus for a long time. Herpes simplex shedding slowly with no signs, yet still transmissible.

9Ch. 13aflashcard13a.1
  • textbook

Protozoa

Back

Single-celled eukaryotes that cause disease with toxins or enzymes that stop host cells working: malaria, sleeping sickness, amebic dysentery, giardiasis.

10Ch. 13aflashcard13a.1
  • textbook

Fungus

Back

A eukaryote that secretes digestive enzymes and absorbs the nutrients — in a human, digesting body cells. Lungs: histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis. Skin: athlete's foot, ringworm.

11Ch. 13aflashcard13a.1
  • textbook

Parasites (parasitic worms)

Back

Multicellular animals living closely with a host that they harm but usually do not kill — flukes, tapeworms, roundworms. They release toxins, feed on blood or compete for food. Example: ascariasis.

12Ch. 13aflashcard13a.1
  • textbook
  • lecture

Prion

Back

An infectious, misfolded protein that makes the normal nerve-cell protein misfold too, leaving spongelike holes in the brain (TSEs: mad cow disease, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease). Not destroyed by heat; no treatment.

13Ch. 13aflashcard13a.2
  • textbook

Five routes by which disease spreads

Back

Direct contact, indirect (droplet) contact, contaminated food or water, animal vectors, shared needles (intravenous drug use).

14Ch. 13aflashcard13a.2
  • textbook

Vector

Back

An animal that carries a disease from one host to another — the deer tick (Lyme disease), the mosquito (West Nile virus).

15Ch. 13aflashcard13a.3
  • textbook

Epidemiology

Back

The study of patterns of disease — rate of occurrence, distribution and control. Epidemiologists are the "disease detectives" who trace an outbreak to its cause.

16Ch. 13aflashcard13a.3
  • textbook

Sporadic disease

Back

Occurs occasionally, at unpredictable intervals, in a few people in a restricted area.

17Ch. 13aflashcard13a.3
  • textbook

Endemic disease

Back

Always present in a population and of little threat — the common cold.

18Ch. 13aflashcard13a.3
  • textbook

Epidemic disease

Back

Occurs suddenly and spreads rapidly to many people — smallpox and cholera outbreaks.

19Ch. 13aflashcard13a.3
  • textbook

Pandemic disease

Back

A global outbreak — HIV/AIDS.

20Ch. 13aflashcard13a.3
  • textbook

Emerging vs reemerging disease

Back

Emerging — clinically distinct, incidence rising (HIV, SARS, H1N1). Reemerging — returns after declining (TB, through drug-resistant strains).

Ch. 14 — The Respiratory System

Week 15 · study page · 37 multiple choice · 0 short answer · 6 flashcards

1Ch. 1414.4 Respiratory centers
  • textbook

Aortic bodies are which type of receptor?

Answer: c

The aortic bodies (on the aorta) and carotid bodies (on the arteries to the head) are peripheral chemoreceptors: they sense blood chemistry — rising CO₂ and H⁺, and dangerously low oxygen — and signal the medulla's breathing center.

2Ch. 1414.2 Lung volumes
  • textbook

Which of these lung volumes is the smallest?

Answer: d

Tidal volume, one quiet breath, is about 500 ml. Expiratory reserve is about 1000 ml, residual volume 1100–1200 ml, inspiratory reserve 1900–3300 ml, and vital capacity (tidal + both reserves) about 3400–4800 ml.

3Ch. 1414.2 Mechanism of breathing
  • textbook

Paralysis of which muscles would stop ventilation?

Answer: b

Inhalation is driven by both the diaphragm (flattens, enlarging the chest top to bottom) and the intercostals (lift the ribs up and out, enlarging it front to back). Lose only one and the other still changes chest volume; lose both and nothing enlarges the chest. Exhalation is passive recoil, so without inhalation there is no ventilation. The pectorals are only accessory muscles that help in forced inspiration (Lab 14 board) — with the diaphragm gone, the intercostals would still move air, so d is wrong.

4Ch. 1414.1 Alveoli
  • textbook

A newborn cannot produce enough surfactant. What is most likely to happen?

Answer: b

Surfactant disrupts the surface tension that would pull the moist alveolar walls together. It is made from the eighth month of fetal life, so premature babies without enough get respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) — the alveoli collapse after each breath. Cystic fibrosis is genetic, and mucus, not surfactant, traps microbes in the nose.

5Ch. 1414.1 Pharynx
  • textbook
  • lecture

The auditory (Eustachian) tube connects which two spaces?

Answer: c

The auditory tubes run from the pharynx to the middle ear and equalise the middle ear's pressure with the outside air. The inner ear is fluid-filled and sealed behind the oval window; the sinuses drain into the nasal cavities, not the ear.

6Ch. 1414.1 Upper vs lower tract
  • textbook

Which of these is not part of the upper respiratory tract?

Answer: b

The upper respiratory system is the nose, nasal cavity, sinuses and pharynx (the book also places the larynx there in Table 14.1, though its §14.1 text puts it lower — see the tab's CONFLICT). The trachea begins the lower respiratory system, with the bronchi, bronchioles and lungs.

7Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • textbook
detail

Which disease is characterized by a high fever, muscle aches and a sore throat?

Answer: d

Influenza hits suddenly with chills, a fever around 103°F, back and muscle aches, headache, sore throat and a dry cough. Strep throat gives a sore throat, swollen lymph nodes and fever but not the body aches; pneumonia is fever, chest pain and shortness of breath from fluid-filled alveoli; TB is a lung infection spread by cough droplets.

8Ch. 1414.1 Sinuses
  • textbook

Which best describes a sinus?

Answer: b

Sinuses are air-filled spaces in the facial bones, connected to and draining into the nasal cavities. They lighten the head, help warm and moisten air, and add to the voice's resonance. The nose-to-ear link is the auditory tube (and it runs from the pharynx); olfactory receptors lie high in the nasal cavities.

9Ch. 1414.3 Gas transport
  • textbook
  • lab manual
  • lecture
said it’s on the exam

What is the main way oxygen travels in the blood?

Answer: b

Oxygen dissolves poorly in water, so 98.5% rides bound to hemoglobin (on the iron of each heme) and only 1.5% is dissolved in plasma. Bicarbonate and carbonic acid belong to carbon dioxide transport.

In lecture: "you need to know the ways the gases are transported and the percentages of each type transport- use your textbook for percentages-These are the numbers you will be tested on" — Lab 14 document, Gas Transport video

10Ch. 1414.1 Larynx
  • textbook
detail

What is true about voice production?

Answer: c
