In laryngitis the vocal cords swell and thicken, cannot vibrate freely, and the voice deepens or fails. Pitch rises with tension — stretched cords are thinner and tighter — so a and b are reversed. The vocal cords vibrate; the glottis is only the opening between them (d).

11Ch. 1414.3 Gas transport
  • textbook

Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes which reaction?

Answer: b

In the tissues, CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid), which then splits into HCO₃⁻ + H⁺. Carbonic anhydrase, found in red blood cells but not plasma, speeds that first step — the book says the reaction runs hundreds of times faster in red cells; in the lungs it runs the reverse, turning carbonic acid back into CO₂ and water to be exhaled.

12Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • textbook
  • lecture

Which disease is characterized by thick, sticky mucus?

Answer: d

Cystic fibrosis is an inherited single-gene disorder: abnormal Cl⁻ channels (the deck's cause) make thick, sticky mucus that clogs the airways and traps bacteria. Chronic bronchitis brings excess mucus too, but it is defined by inflamed bronchi and a long-lasting productive cough, usually from smoking — the inherited "thick, sticky mucus" disease is CF; emphysema breaks down alveoli; pneumonia fills alveoli with fluid.

13Ch. 1414.1 Larynx
  • textbook
detail

What is likely to happen if a person has an inflamed epiglottis?

Answer: d

A swollen epiglottis sits right over the glottis, the only opening air passes through into the larynx, so inflammation can block the airway and stop breathing. This is the homework's keyed answer; the Ch. 14 tab covers the epiglottis only as the lid that keeps food out during swallowing, which is why "food can enter the lower airway" is the tempting wrong pick.

14Ch. 1414.1 Respiration
  • textbook

In physiological terms, what does gas transport mean?

Answer: c

Respiration is four processes: breathing, external respiration (lungs ↔ blood), gas transport (the blood carries O₂ to the cells and CO₂ to the lungs) and internal respiration (blood ↔ tissue cells). Moving air nose → lungs is breathing (ventilation); diffusing down a gradient is how the two exchange steps work.

15Ch. 1414.1 Airway
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A piece of food gets lodged directly below the larynx. Which structure is it stuck in?

Answer: d

Air passes pharynx → larynx (opening: glottis) → trachea → primary bronchi → bronchioles. The trachea begins directly below the larynx. The pharynx is above it, the glottis is the larynx's own opening, and the bronchi branch off the bottom of the trachea.

16Ch. 1414.3 Lung volumes
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What is the maximum amount of air that can be inhaled or exhaled in a single breath called?

Answer: b

Vital capacity = inspiratory reserve + tidal volume + expiratory reserve: all the air that can be moved in one breath. Tidal volume is one quiet breath (about 500 mL). Residual volume never leaves the lungs. Inspiratory reserve is only the extra air in after a normal breath in.

17Ch. 1414.1 Larynx
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which structure covers the larynx during swallowing?

Answer: c

The epiglottis folds down over the glottis, the opening of the larynx, so food goes to the esophagus instead of the airway. The glottis is the opening being covered, and the Adam's apple is the larynx's own cartilage.

18Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • textbook

A patient arrives with a "barrel chest" and trouble breathing. What is the likely cause?

Answer: c

A barrel chest is the classic sign of emphysema. Alveolar walls break down into fewer, larger spaces that are hard to empty, so air is trapped (residual volume rises) and the chest stays over-inflated. Ch. 14 names tobacco as the commonest US cause of COPD (bronchitis and emphysema). Infections cause pneumonia and colds, not this; the genetic disease in the chapter is cystic fibrosis (thick mucus).

19Ch. 1414.4 Control of breathing
  • textbook

What is the main stimulus that activates the central chemoreceptors?

Answer: b

The central chemoreceptors sit in the medulla, bathed in cerebrospinal fluid. CO₂ diffuses into that fluid and forms carbonic acid, which releases H⁺, and the H⁺ is what stimulates them (CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻). Rising CO₂ is the cause, which makes "increased CO₂" the tempting second choice on the homework, but the receptors respond to H⁺. Low oxygen is sensed only by the carotid and aortic bodies, and only when it is dangerously low.

20Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Asthma is mainly a problem with which part of the airway?

Answer: d

In asthma the smooth muscle in the airway walls spasms and inflammation narrows the airways. The bronchioles have no cartilage, so they are the airways that can constrict, and that is why they are the site of an asthma attack (the lab says the same: bronchiole smooth muscle constricts). The trachea and bronchi are held open by cartilage, and the pleural membranes line the lungs and chest wall. The alveoli are the exchange surface, and emphysema is the disease of the alveoli.

21Ch. 1414.1 Sinuses
  • textbook

Which of the following is not a function of the sinuses?

Answer: c

Ch. 14: the sinuses are air-filled spaces in the skull bones that lighten the head, help warm and moisten inhaled air (they are lined with mucous membrane), and form part of the voice's resonating chamber. Olfaction (smell) belongs to the olfactory receptors high in the nasal cavity. "Lightening the head" is the tempting wrong pick because it sounds too simple to be a real function.

22Ch. 1414.1 Why we breathe
  • textbook

Why must we breathe oxygen?

Answer: a

Cells use O2 in cellular respiration (Ch. 3) as the final electron acceptor, which lets them extract far more ATP from glucose than they could without it; the oxygen ends up in water, so it is not "broken down" for energy (c). The main chemical driving breathing rate is CO2, sensed as H⁺; oxygen matters only when dangerously low (b).

23Ch. 1414.1 Four processes
  • textbook

Which term describes moving oxygen-rich air into the lungs and carbon dioxide-laden air out of them?

Answer: b

Ch. 14 splits respiration into four processes: breathing (ventilating) moves air into and out of the lungs; external respiration exchanges gases between the lungs and the blood; gas transport carries them in the blood; and internal respiration exchanges them between blood and tissue cells. "Respiration" alone is the tempting fill-in, but it names the exchange, not the air movement.

24Ch. 1414.1 Trachea
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What would happen if the trachea had no cartilage rings?

Answer: c

The C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings exist to hold the trachea open so the airway does not collapse as pressure changes during breathing. Humidifying and filtering air are jobs of the nose, sinuses and the ciliated mucous lining, and smell comes from olfactory receptors in the nasal cavity, so none of those depend on the rings.

25Ch. 1414.2 Breathing
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which statement about breathing is correct?

Answer: d

Quiet expiration is passive: the diaphragm and external intercostals relax, the elastic lungs recoil, the chest shrinks, lung pressure rises above atmospheric, and air flows out. Muscles contracting and the chest enlarging (a and c) describe inspiration. The larynx is a passageway and voice box, not a pump.

26Ch. 1414.2 Breathing
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which muscles of the rib cage help enlarge the thoracic cavity during inhalation?

Answer: a

The intercostal muscles (inter, between; costa, rib) lie between the ribs; during inhalation they contract with the diaphragm and pull the rib cage up and out, enlarging the chest front to back. Strictly it is the external intercostals; the internal layer helps in forced exhalation. Abdominals push air out in forced exhalation, and scalenes and pectorals are accessory muscles that join only in forced inhalation and are not rib-cage muscles.

27Ch. 1414.3 Internal respiration
  • textbook
  • lab manual

During exercise, O2 is depleted in muscle tissue. What effect does this have on internal respiration?

Answer: c

Gases diffuse down their partial-pressure gradient. Working muscle uses up O2, so its O2 partial pressure falls further below the blood's: the gradient is steeper, and more O2 diffuses from the systemic capillaries into the tissue. Exercise raises heart rate, and O2 moves from the lungs into the blood, not out (b).

28Ch. 1414.3 Gas transport
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual
said it’s on the exam

How does most carbon dioxide travel in the blood, and about what share?

Answer: c

Whalen's deck (slide 52): CO₂ travels 70% as bicarbonate (an important part of the body's acid–base buffer), 20–23% on hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin, and 7–10% dissolved in plasma. 98.5% is oxygen's figure — the share of O₂ bound to hemoglobin.

In lecture: "you need to know the ways the gases are transported and the percentages of each type transport- use your textbook for percentages-These are the numbers you will be tested on" — Lab 14 document, Gas Transport video

29Ch. 1414.1 Functions
  • lecture
  • textbook

Whalen's deck lists the respiratory system's functions. Which is one of them?

Answer: b

Slide 3: the respiratory system provides oxygen for cellular respiration, removes carbon dioxide (its waste product), and regulates the acid–base balance of body fluids — exhaling CO₂ removes acid. Making red cells and activating vitamin D are kidney jobs (Ch. 16); calcium is stored in bone.

30Ch. 1414.4 Respiratory centers
  • lecture
  • textbook

Where is the breathing center that sets the basic breathing pattern?

Answer: a

The deck (slides 53–54): the breathing center is in the medulla, with inspiratory and expiratory areas. The cerebral cortex can voluntarily change the pattern (holding your breath, speaking), but it does not set it. The carotid bodies are chemoreceptors that report to the medulla.

31Ch. 1414.5 Asthma
  • lecture
  • textbook

What does an asthma inhaler's bronchodilator do?

Answer: c

The deck (slide 31) gives two inhalant treatments: bronchodilators relax the bronchial muscles, reopening the constricted airways, and anti-inflammatories reduce inflammation of the air tubes. Asthma is not a bacterial infection, and surfactant problems are respiratory distress syndrome.

32Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which disease does a bacterium spread by respiratory droplets cause, walled off in the lungs as fibrous tubercles?

Answer: b

Tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spread in respiratory droplets; the lungs wall it off in fibrous tubercles. It can be fatal, and multi-drug-resistant strains are rising (deck slide 65). Pneumonia fills alveoli with fluid; CF is inherited; emphysema destroys alveoli.

33Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Untreated strep throat can lead to which serious consequences?

Answer: c

Strep throat is caused by Streptococcus bacteria (sore throat, swollen glands, fever). Untreated it can cause rheumatic fever or kidney disease — glomerulonephritis (deck slide 64). Emphysema and lung cancer come mainly from smoking; CF is inherited.

34Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • lecture
  • textbook

In pneumonia, what happens in the lungs?

Answer: a

Deck slide 63: pneumonia is an inflammation of the lungs in which fluid accumulates in the alveoli, cutting gas exchange, and the bronchioles swell and narrow; it is most often a bacterial or viral infection. Broken-down alveolar walls are emphysema, thick mucus is cystic fibrosis, and spasm of the bronchial muscles is asthma.

35Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which disorder is an inflammation of the bronchi's mucous membranes, with excess mucus and a deep cough?

Answer: c

Bronchitis (deck slide 68): inflamed mucous membranes of the bronchi, caused by viruses, bacteria or chemical irritation; excess mucus triggers a deep cough; it can be acute or chronic. With emphysema it is one of the two commonest forms of COPD. Laryngitis inflames the larynx, not the bronchi.

36Ch. 1414.5 Lung cancer
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

About what share of lung cancers does Whalen's deck say smoking causes?

Answer: c

Deck slide 71: 85% to 90% of lung cancers are caused by smoking. The progression runs chronic inflammation → changes in the airway-lining cells → uncontrolled division forming a tumor → metastasis to the rest of the lung and body.

37Ch. 1414.5 Disorders
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

How many different viruses can cause the common cold, according to the deck?

Answer: d

Deck slide 60: the common cold is caused by more than 200 different viruses, typically lasts 1 to 2 weeks, and spreads by touching contaminated items and then mucous membranes. The "3 major types" (A, B and C) are the influenza viruses (slide 61).

1Ch. 14flashcard14.1 Pharynx
  • textbook

Pharynx

Back

The part of the upper respiratory system that is a shared passageway for food and air.

2Ch. 14flashcard14.1 Trachea
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Trachea

Back

Connects the larynx to the bronchi; held open by C-shaped cartilage rings.

3Ch. 14flashcard14.1 Bronchioles
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Bronchioles

Back

Narrow airways carrying air from the bronchi to the alveoli; no cartilage.

4Ch. 14flashcard14.5 Disorders
  • textbook

Emphysema

Back

The walls of the alveoli break down: fewer, larger air spaces, less exchange surface, trapped air (residual volume rises).

5Ch. 14flashcard14.2 Lung volumes
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Inspiratory reserve vs expiratory reserve

Back

Inspiratory reserve: extra air you can breathe in after a normal breath in. Expiratory reserve: extra air you can force out after a normal breath out.

6Ch. 14flashcard14.2 Breathing
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Diaphragm

Back

Muscle sheet separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities; contracts and flattens to inflate the lungs.

Ch. 16 — The Urinary System

Week 15 · study page · 31 multiple choice · 0 short answer

1Ch. 1616.3 Juxtaglomerular apparatus
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What is true about the juxtaglomerular apparatus?

Answer: a

The juxtaglomerular apparatus is where the distal tubule touches the afferent arteriole. When pressure in the afferent arteriole drops, its cells release renin, which starts the chain to angiotensin II and aldosterone and raises blood pressure. So it is the DCT, not the PCT (c); it is triggered by low pressure (b); and it raises pressure, not lowers it (d). The pressure-sensing cells are in the afferent arteriole, not the efferent one.

2Ch. 1616.3 Water balance
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A person who is well hydrated will make a ______ volume of urine that is ______.

Answer: c

With plenty of water in the blood, the posterior pituitary releases little ADH, so the collecting ducts reabsorb less water. The kidneys excrete a large volume of dilute (hypotonic) urine. A dehydrated person is the reverse: high ADH, a small volume of concentrated (hypertonic) urine.

3Ch. 1616.5 Kidney failure
  • textbook

Which of the following is not a consequence of renal failure?

Answer: b

Healthy kidneys release erythropoietin, which stimulates red blood cell production, so failing kidneys cause anemia, not extra red cells. The rest all follow from kidneys that cannot do their jobs: urea is not excreted, so blood urea nitrogen rises; water and salt are retained, causing edema and hypertension; and H⁺ is not secreted, so the blood becomes acidic.

4Ch. 1616.2 Urination
  • textbook

Which shows the correct order of events for urination?

Answer: b

Stretch receptors in the filling bladder trigger a spinal reflex: the detrusor (the bladder's smooth muscle) contracts and the internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle, involuntary) relaxes. Urine leaves only when the brain then relaxes the external urethral sphincter, which is skeletal muscle under voluntary control. Option a puts the brain step first; c swaps which step is voluntary; d has every muscle doing the opposite.

5Ch. 1616.4 Kidney functions
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which organ stimulates red blood cell production and regulates blood pH?

Answer: d

The kidneys release erythropoietin, which stimulates the red bone marrow to make red blood cells, and they regulate pH by secreting H⁺ and reabsorbing bicarbonate. The marrow makes the cells but does not regulate pH. The lungs affect pH by exhaling CO₂ but do not control red cell production. The bladder only stores urine.

6Ch. 1616.3 Nephron loop
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What is the function of the descending limb of the nephron loop?

Answer: b

The descending limb is permeable to water but not to salt, so water leaves it by osmosis into the salty tissue of the medulla. The ascending limb is the reverse: it moves NaCl out but is impermeable to water. Renin comes from the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

7Ch. 1616.3 Reabsorption
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which of the following would not be reabsorbed from the filtrate?

Answer: c

Creatinine is a nitrogen-containing waste from muscle metabolism, so it stays in the filtrate and leaves in the urine; the PCT even secretes more of it. Useful substances are reclaimed: all the glucose, most water and sodium, and bicarbonate, which also helps regulate blood pH.

8Ch. 1616.3 ADH
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) targets which part of the kidney?

Answer: b

ADH from the posterior pituitary makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water (by adding aquaporins), so more water is reabsorbed and the urine is concentrated. Sources disagree: the lab and Whalen's deck (slide 35) say ADH acts on the DCT and collecting ducts, while Ch. 16 names the collecting ducts only. With only the collecting ducts offered, as here, that is the answer. The PCT and nephron loop reabsorb water without hormonal control, and the glomerulus only filters.

9Ch. 1616.3 Filtration
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which of the following should not normally be found in the filtrate?

Answer: b

In filtration, blood pressure pushes water and small solutes (ions such as sodium, potassium and bicarbonate, plus glucose, amino acids and urea) out of the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule. Blood cells and most proteins are too large to pass, so they stay in the blood. Red cells or protein in the urine signal a damaged filter.

10Ch. 1616.5 Kidney failure
  • textbook

Which is not associated with acute renal failure?

Answer: b

Acute renal failure is an abrupt loss of kidney function over hours or days, often with little urine; it can follow severe inflammation, drugs, poison, blood loss or kidney stones. The slow decline over months or years is chronic renal failure. Either kind brings the same consequences: anemia (no erythropoietin), acidosis (H⁺ not excreted), hypertension and edema, and rising nitrogenous wastes.

11Ch. 1616.2 Urination
  • textbook

What is true about the detrusor muscle?

Answer: c

The detrusor is the smooth muscle of the bladder wall. In the urination reflex it contracts while the internal sphincter relaxes, pushing urine into the urethra. The external urethral sphincter is a separate band of skeletal muscle under voluntary control, and the ureters move urine to the bladder by peristalsis of their own smooth muscle.

12Ch. 1616.3 Secretion
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which of the following would be secreted into the filtrate?

Answer: d

Secretion moves substances from the blood into the tubule to be excreted: H⁺, ammonium, creatinine, potassium and drugs such as penicillin. Secreting H⁺ keeps the blood from becoming acidic. Bicarbonate, glucose, sodium and most water go the other way: they are reabsorbed into the blood.

13Ch. 1616.3 Reabsorption
  • textbook

A person is born without microvilli on the kidney tubule cells. Which process will be impacted most?

Answer: c

Microvilli line the proximal convoluted tubule, multiplying its surface area for reabsorption: the PCT reclaims the most of any segment, including all the glucose and amino acids, most ions and much of the water. Filtration happens across the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule, which have no microvilli. Choosing filtration is the common slip, because both words describe the nephron's first steps.

14Ch. 1616.3 Filtration
  • textbook
  • lab manual

What is the function of the glomerulus?

Answer: b

The glomerulus is a ball of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule. Blood pressure pushes water and small solutes out of it into the capsule, which is filtration, forming the filtrate. Reabsorption and secretion happen later, along the tubules, and pH is adjusted there by secreting H⁺ and reclaiming bicarbonate. ADH comes from the posterior pituitary.

15Ch. 1616.3 Aldosterone
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Aldosterone causes ______.

Answer: c

Aldosterone, from the adrenal cortex, acts on the DCT and collecting duct to reabsorb more sodium and secrete more potassium (it also drives H⁺ secretion). Water follows the sodium, so blood volume and pressure rise. Every other option reverses at least one of the two ions.

16Ch. 1616.2 Kidney anatomy
  • textbook
  • lab manual
detail

Renal columns separate ______ from ______.

Answer: b

The renal medulla is divided into cone-shaped renal pyramids. Renal columns are extensions of cortex tissue that dip inward between adjacent pyramids, separating one pyramid from the next. The cortex and medulla are separate regions with no column between them, and the pelvis is the funnel the pyramids drain into.

17Ch. 1616.2 Urinary tract
  • textbook
  • lab manual

A kidney stone lodges in the ureter. Urine will not be able to go from the ______ to the ______.

Answer: b

Urine runs kidney (collecting ducts → renal pelvis) → ureter → urinary bladder → urethra → outside. Each ureter carries urine from a kidney to the bladder, so a stone lodged there blocks that step. Option a is the right pair in reverse. The collecting ducts and pelvis lie upstream, inside the kidney, and the urethra lies downstream, below the bladder.

18Ch. 1616.3 ANH
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which is not true about atrial natriuretic hormone (ANH)?

Answer: b

The atria of the heart release ANH (the lab calls it ANP) when rising blood volume stretches them, that is, when pressure is too high. ANH works against the RAAS: it cuts sodium reabsorption, suppresses renin (and so aldosterone), and makes the kidneys excrete more salt and water, giving more urine and lower blood volume and pressure.

19Ch. 1616.1 Excretion
  • textbook

Which organ systems eliminate urea and uric acid?

Answer: c

The kidneys (urinary system) are the main route for nitrogen-containing wastes: urea, uric acid and creatinine leave in urine. The skin (integumentary system) also excretes salts and a little urea and uric acid in sweat. The lungs eliminate CO₂, water and heat, and the gut eliminates feces, so neither handles these two wastes.

20Ch. 1616.1 Excretion
  • textbook

Which element do urea, uric acid and creatinine all contain?

Answer: c

All three are the nitrogen-containing wastes: urea is made in the liver from ammonia (protein breakdown), uric acid from recycling nucleotide bases, and creatinine from the breakdown of creatine phosphate in muscle. The kidneys are the main route for removing them.

21Ch. 1616.3 Urine formation
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which processes in the nephron cause a waste product from the blood to end up in urine?

Answer: c

A waste enters the tubule two ways: filtration at the glomerulus pushes it out of the blood with the filtrate, and tubular secretion moves more of it from the peritubular blood into the tubule (H⁺, creatinine, drugs). Reabsorption works the other way, returning useful substances from the filtrate to the blood.

22Ch. 1616.4 pH balance
  • textbook

A person skips his insulin and develops diabetic ketoacidosis. What will his body do to correct the low blood pH?

Answer: b

Two systems correct acidic blood. The kidneys secrete more H⁺ into the urine (and reclaim bicarbonate, a buffer). The lungs breathe faster and deeper, blowing off CO₂; since CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻, less CO₂ means less H⁺. Rising H⁺ is exactly what the chemoreceptors sense to speed up breathing (Ch. 14). Decreasing ventilation would keep CO₂ in and lower pH further.

23Ch. 1616.2 Kidney anatomy
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which structure most directly drains into the renal pelvis?

Answer: c

Filtrate runs renal corpuscle → PCT → nephron loop → DCT → collecting duct, and the collecting ducts run through the pyramids to empty into the renal pelvis (the lab adds the minor and major calyces as the cups in between). The ureter is downstream: it carries urine from the pelvis to the bladder.

24Ch. 1616.4 Dialysis
  • lecture
  • textbook

What is the difference between hemodialysis and CAPD?

Answer: b

Deck slide 44: hemodialysis cleanses the blood with artificial devices, such as an artificial kidney machine. Continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) uses the patient's own peritoneum as the dialyzing membrane, done at home. A donor kidney is a transplant — the deck's "ultimate hope".

25Ch. 1616.5 Urination
  • lecture
  • textbook

Which pairing of urination problem and definition is correct?

Answer: c

Deck slide 49: urinary incontinence is a lack of voluntary control over urination — normal in infants and toddlers; stress incontinence is more common in women. Urinary retention is a failure to expel urine from the bladder to a normal degree. Options a and b swap the two.

26Ch. 1616.6 UTIs
  • lecture
  • textbook

Why are urinary tract infections more common in women than in men?

Answer: b

Whalen (Wed 11/18): UTIs are more frequent in females "for one reason, and only one reason" — the female urethra is only about 4 cm, the male's about 20 cm, so bacteria have a short climb to the bladder. The deck (slides 50, 52) says the same, and adds that bacteria can enter the urethra from the rectum or as STDs.

27Ch. 1616.6 UTIs
  • lecture
  • textbook

Why are UTIs treated promptly with antibiotics?

Answer: a

Deck slide 51: UTI symptoms include fever, blood in the urine, and painful, frequent urination; antibiotics treat an infection of the lower urinary tract (urethra, bladder) to prevent its spread to the kidneys. Raising urine pH would help bacteria, not stop them (Whalen, Wed 11/18).

28Ch. 1616.6 UTIs
  • lecture

In lecture, why did Whalen warn against "cleanses" that make urine alkaline?

Answer: b

Whalen (Wed 11/18): normal urine "should be acidic", around pH 6, which is an inhospitable environment for microbes, and urine should be sterile; every urination flushes bacteria out of the urethra. "If you neutralize your urine, what you're doing is saying, hey, bacteria, it's okay for you to be here."

29Ch. 1616.3 Water conservation
  • lecture
  • textbook
detail

Which nephrons, with long loops reaching deep into the renal medulla, are responsible for conserving water?

Answer: b

Deck slide 28: juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops that extend into the medulla and are responsible for conserving water. The medulla keeps a high solute concentration, so water moves out of the descending loop, DCT and collecting ducts, producing concentrated urine (slide 29).

30Ch. 1616.3 Hormones
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which three hormones does Whalen's deck name as adjusting the kidney's handling of salt and water?

Answer: c

Slide 31: aldosterone (adrenal cortex; reabsorb Na⁺, secrete K⁺), ADH (posterior pituitary; water permeability) and ANP (right atrium; less Na⁺ reabsorption, dilute urine). Renin is an enzyme from the JGA, and erythropoietin and calcitriol are the kidney's other products, not water-balance hormones acting on it.

31Ch. 1616.3 Aldosterone
  • lecture
  • textbook
  • lab manual

Which of these does not trigger aldosterone release, according to Whalen's deck?

Answer: d

Deck slide 32: aldosterone's stimuli are low blood pressure (the RAAS, monitored by the juxtaglomerular apparatus), stress (more ACTH) and increased K⁺. A rise in blood volume and pressure triggers ANP instead, which inhibits renin and aldosterone (slides 38–39).

Lab 12 — Blood & Immunity

Week 14 · study page · 52 multiple choice · 9 short answer · 29 flashcards

1Lab 12Activity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

You spin a capillary tube of blood and see a thin whitish band between the two main layers. What is that band?

Answer: b

Buffy coat — white blood cells plus platelets, about 1 mm, under 1% of the column. Plasma (a) is the straw-coloured top layer, about 55%; the packed RBCs (c) sit at the bottom, about 45%. The anticoagulant is there to stop clotting, so there is no clot (d).

In lecture: "Be able to break down the composition of the blood 55% of total blood volume is plasma, the other 45% would call the formed element." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

2Lab 12Activity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual

A blood column measures 50 mm in total and its red layer measures 21 mm. Using the lab's formula, what is the hematocrit?

Answer: c

HCT = (RBC volume ÷ total blood volume) × 100% = 21 ÷ 50 × 100 = 42%. Option a reads the RBC height as if it were a percentage; 29 mm (b) is the plasma height, not a percentage; 58% (d) is the plasma share. 42% sits in both the lab's female (37–47%) and male (42–52%) ranges.

3Lab 12Activity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

In a normal spun sample, what share of the total blood volume is plasma?

Answer: b

Plasma about 55%, RBCs about 45% (the hematocrit), buffy coat under 1%. 93% (d) is the share of plasma itself that is water, per Whalen's Ch. 11 deck — a different number.

In lecture: "Be able to break down the composition of the blood 55% of total blood volume is plasma, the other 45% would call the formed element." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

4Lab 12Activity 1 · Blood componentsselect all that apply
  • lab manual

Which statements about the components of blood are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, d, e

The lab's own summary question. Plasma carries electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, gases and wastes (a). The buffy coat is WBCs + platelets, and it — not the RBCs — is the smallest layer, under 1% (so b is false: RBCs are about 45%). Low HCT = anemia (d); high HCT = polycythemia, but dehydration falsely raises it and is the most common cause of a high reading (e).

5Lab 12Activity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual

After a day of vomiting with no fluids, a patient's hematocrit reads 56%. What does the lab say is the most likely explanation?

Answer: b

Plasma is the difference between RBC volume and total volume, so losing plasma water raises the HCT without adding a single red cell — the lab calls dehydration the most common cause of a high HCT. True polycythemia (a) is a real excess of RBCs. Anemia (c) lowers HCT; fluid overload (d) also lowers it.

6Lab 12Activity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual
detail

Which pair of normal hematocrit ranges matches the lab?

Answer: b

Female 37–47%, male 42–52% — males run higher. Option a is the exact swap. (The lab document also asks for a reason for the difference; none of the course material gives one, so this bank does not supply one.)

7Lab 12Activity 1 · Plasma
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A patient's blood albumin is very low. Which job of the plasma proteins suffers most?

Answer: a

Albumin — fluid balance, keeping water in the vessels; it is over half the plasma proteins. Globulins carry lipids and vitamins (α, β) and are antibodies (γ) — options b and d. Fibrinogen is the clotting protein (c).

8Lab 12Activity 1 · Blood components
  • lab manual
  • textbook

In the lab's table of blood portions, which pairing of portion and function is correct?

Answer: c

Plasma transports nutrients, hormones, gases and wastes (and its proteins balance fluid, carry lipids, act as antibodies and clot). Erythrocytes carry oxygen (a has it on the wrong layer); the buffy coat defends — its WBCs — and clots — its platelets (b puts defense on the wrong layer). Engulfing (d) is phagocytosis, which only cells do — the WBCs of the buffy coat, not the fluid plasma.

9Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On a stained smear you find a cell with a nucleus of two lobes and large red-orange granules. What is it?

Answer: d

Eosinophil — two lobes, red-orange (eosin-pink) granules. Neutrophil (a): 2–5 lobes, pale lilac granules. Basophil (b): dense dark-purple granules. Monocyte (c): the largest, kidney-shaped nucleus, no visible granules.

10Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

The largest white cell on the smear has a kidney-shaped nucleus and no visible granules. What does it become once it leaves the blood?

Answer: b

That is a monocyte, an agranulocyte; in tissue it becomes a macrophage — a phagocyte that secretes cytokines and acts as an APC. Plasma cells (a) come from B lymphocytes. Mast cells (c) are tissue cells related to basophils. Megakaryocytes (d) are marrow cells that fragment into platelets.

11Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On a smear, which description matches a lymphocyte?

Answer: a

Lymphocyte — a large round nucleus almost filling the cell, little cytoplasm. Option b is a neutrophil, c a monocyte, d a basophil.

12Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Going by the lab's list of phagocytes, which set is made up only of phagocytic cells?

Answer: b

The lab's phagocytes are neutrophils, eosinophils and macrophages (monocytes become macrophages, and the glossary lists monocytes as phagocytes too, so "neutrophils, monocytes and eosinophils" would also be accepted). Basophils, like mast cells, are not phagocytic — they release histamine, which is why the lab's own select-all item "basophils, neutrophils and macrophages are all phagocytic" is false (a). Sources differ on eosinophils: the lab and Whalen's deck count them as phagocytes; the Ch. 11 table has them engulf antibody–antigen complexes; but the §13.2 text says they attack pathogens "too big to engulf" and Table 13.1 lists them apart from the phagocytes. For the lab exam, include them.

13Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cellsselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statements about blood cells are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b, e

The lab's own summary question. RBCs carry O2 and about 23% of the CO2 (a). Neutrophils are the most numerous WBC (b). Basophils are not phagocytic (c). Platelets are for clotting (hemostasis), not immunity (d). B lymphocytes give rise to plasma cells, which make antibodies (e). T lymphocytes are adaptive — the third line, not the first (f); the first line is skin, mucous membranes and their chemicals.

14Lab 12Activity 2 · Cell definitions
  • lab manual

In the lab's cell-definition table, which cell "displays antigens to activate T cells"?

Answer: d

Dendritic cell — a phagocyte that displays antigen on its MHC proteins; the glossary calls dendritic cells the most common APC. Macrophages and B cells can present too. Mast cells release histamine; NK cells kill infected and abnormal cells; plasma cells make antibodies.

15Lab 12Activity 2 · Cell definitions
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Both cells release histamine. Which is the one that sits in the tissues, rather than circulating in the blood?

Answer: b

The lab's table pairs them: basophil — releases histamine, circulates in the bloodstream; mast cell — releases histamine, located in the tissue. The textbook calls mast cells small, mobile connective-tissue cells. Eosinophils target parasites; neutrophils are the first-responding phagocytes.

16Lab 12Activity 2 · Cell definitions
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A virus-infected cell is killed within hours of infection, before any antigen-specific lymphocyte has been activated. Which cell most likely killed it?

Answer: c

NK cells are innate and non-specific — they look for any suspicious cell (infected, cancerous) and kill it with perforins + granzymes, triggering apoptosis. Cytotoxic T cells (a) kill the same targets, but only after antigen-specific activation, which takes days. Helper T cells activate; plasma cells make antibodies.

17Lab 12Activity 2 · Adaptive cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which adaptive-immunity cell activates both B cells and cytotoxic T cells?

Answer: d

Helper T — the switch for both branches. In the lab's terms, effector helper T cells release IL-2 (activating cytotoxic T) and IL-2, IL-4, IL-5 (fully activating a B cell). Memory B cells wait for a repeat exposure; plasma cells make antibodies; NK cells are innate.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend… you understand and know this table." — the table of adaptive-response cells (helper, cytotoxic and suppressor T cells, B cells, plasma cells, memory cells), Wed 11/18

18Lab 12Activity 2 · Adaptive cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Why is the response to a second exposure to the same pathogen faster and bigger than the first?

Answer: a

Memory B and T cells remain after the first infection; they are far more numerous than the original naive cells and each clones into new effector and memory cells. Effector cells live only days (c is backwards), so plasma cells (b) and their antibodies (d) fall once the invader is gone.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend… you understand and know this table." — the table of adaptive-response cells (helper, cytotoxic and suppressor T cells, B cells, plasma cells, memory cells), Wed 11/18

19Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

A drug blocks thrombopoietin. Which formed element would fall?

Answer: c

Thrombopoietin stimulates platelet production — platelets are fragments of megakaryocytes in red bone marrow. Red cell production is driven by a different hormone, erythropoietin, from the kidney (a).

20Lab 12Activity 3 · Blood typing
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A typing card shows agglutination in the anti-B well only — none in the anti-A or anti-D wells. What is the blood type?

Answer: d

Clumping = that antigen is present. Anti-B clumps → B antigen; anti-A clear → no A; anti-D clear → no Rh, so Rh−. B+ (a) would also clump in anti-D; AB− (c) would clump in anti-A too.

In lecture: "Explain how antibodies and antigen help determine blood type." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

21Lab 12Activity 3 · Blood typing
  • lab manual
  • textbook

According to the lab's blood-type table, which antibodies does a person with B− blood have?

Answer: b

The lab's table: B− → antigen B; antibodies anti-A, anti-Rh. Anti-B (c, d) would attack the person's own cells. But the sources disagree on the anti-Rh: the lab's own text and Ch. 11 §11.4 say anti-Rh forms only after an Rh− person is exposed to Rh antigen — so on the textbook's terms a never-exposed B− person carries anti-A only (a). Answer the lab's table on the lab exam; know the exposure rule for the lecture exam (next question).

22Lab 12Activity 3 · Rh vs ABO antibodies
  • textbook
  • lab manual

An Rh− man has never had a transfusion. According to Ch. 11, does his plasma contain anti-Rh antibodies?

Answer: b

Anti-A and anti-B are present without exposure; anti-Rh is not — it forms only after an Rh− person meets Rh antigen (a transfusion, or Rh+ fetal cells at delivery). That is why a first mistaken Rh+ transfusion causes no reaction but a second one can kill. Option c is how the lab's table reads, which conflicts with its own text; d is wrong — exposed Rh− people do make it.

23Lab 12Activity 3 · Blood typingselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which statements about agglutination in a blood typing test are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, e, f

The lab's own summary question. Antigens are on the red cells; the typing sera add antibodies — so b has it backwards. Each well tests its own antigen: A well → A, B well → B (so d is false), D well → Rh. No clumping means the antigen is absent (e).

In lecture: "Explain how antibodies and antigen help determine blood type." — his Ch. 11 objectives slide, read aloud, Mon 11/09

24Lab 12Activity 3 · Donor and recipientselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A person with A+ blood can donate red cells to which recipients? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, d

Donor cells carry A and Rh. The recipient must have no anti-A and no anti-Rh: A+ (anti-B only) and AB+ (no antibodies). B and O types carry anti-A; every Rh− type is ruled out — by the lab's table they carry anti-Rh, and by Ch. 11 an Rh− person should receive only Rh− blood.

25Lab 12Activity 3 · Donor and recipient
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A type A patient is given type B red cells by mistake. What causes the dangerous transfusion reaction?

Answer: a

Ask: what antigens are on the donor cells, and what antibodies are in the recipient? B cells meet her anti-B → agglutination, a transfusion reaction that can be fatal (clumps block small vessels; burst cells release hemoglobin that clogs the kidneys). Type A carries anti-B, not anti-A (d). On the donor's antibodies (b) the sources differ: Ch. 11 says they are diluted and "not a major problem" (and packed red cells carry little plasma); the lab cross-matches in both directions anyway. Either way, the reaction that matters is the recipient's antibodies against the donor's cells.

26Lab 12Activity 3 · Rh vs ABO antibodies
  • lab manual
  • textbook

According to the lab, why can anti-Rh antibodies reach a fetus?

Answer: d

The lab: anti-A and anti-B are large IgM; anti-Rh is small IgG, which crosses the placenta. Table 13.4 agrees that IgG is the class that crosses. The mother makes it (b); red cells cannot cross the placenta (c). This is the basis of hemolytic disease of the newborn in an Rh− mother's second Rh+ pregnancy.

27Lab 12Activity 4 · Barrier defenses
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which of these is NOT one of the first-line barrier defenses?

Answer: d

Interferons are second-line defensive proteins — an infected cell's warning to its neighbours. The first line keeps pathogens out: skin, mucous membranes and mucus, and chemicals — lysozyme (tears, saliva, sweat), low pH (stomach, sweat, urine) — plus normal flora.

28Lab 12Activity 4 · Barrier defenses
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Where are mucous membranes found, and how do they stop pathogens?

Answer: c

Mucous membranes line the digestive and respiratory passages (the immunology glossary adds the urogenital tract), and their sticky mucus traps pathogens; the glossary adds that mucus contains antimicrobial enzymes and antibodies, and in the upper airway cilia sweep it to the throat. Option a is the skin; b is inflammation; d is the lymph nodes.

29Lab 12Activity 4 · Barrier defenses
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which antimicrobial enzyme do tears, saliva and sweat all carry?

Answer: a

Lysozyme kills some bacteria by disrupting their cell walls. Histamine (b) is the mast cell and basophil signal for inflammation; perforin (c) is what NK and cytotoxic T cells use to hole a target; fibrinogen (d) is a clotting protein. (The textbook names tears and saliva; the lab adds sweat.)

30Lab 12Activity 4 · Antigens and antibodies
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statement correctly distinguishes an antigen from an antibody?

Answer: d

Antigen — a molecule (protein, polysaccharide, nucleic acid…) recognized by its shape that triggers an immune response. Antibody — a Y-shaped protein (immunoglobulin) made by plasma cells that binds one specific antigen. Option b is the swap; in blood typing the antigens are on the red cells and the antibodies in the plasma (c is backwards).

31Lab 12Activity 4 · Antigens and antibodies
  • lab manual
  • textbook

True or false, from the lab: "Antigens are found on pathogens and are not on human body cells."

Answer: b

False. The blood-type markers the lab types for — A, B and Rh — are antigens on your own red cells; the immunology glossary also defines self-antigens, and in the lab every nucleated cell shows its own (endogenous) antigen on MHC I. Watch the textbook's wording: Ch. 13 §13.3 defines an antigen as a nonself substance that triggers a response, which makes option a look right — but Ch. 11 itself calls the A, B and Rh markers antigens.

32Lab 12Activity 4 · Lymphoid organs
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which pairing of lymphoid organ and function is correct?

Answer: c

Bone marrow — contains the blood stem cells that give rise to RBCs and every immune cell · lymph nodes — filter pathogens from the lymph (macrophages and lymphocytes inside) · spleen — removes old, damaged cells from the blood (red pulp) · thymus — where T cells mature. Each wrong option moves one function to the wrong organ.

33Lab 12Activity 4 · Lymphoid organs
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What happens to T cells during their maturation in the thymus?

Answer: c

Each T cell is programmed during development for one antigen, carrying thousands of identical receptors; in the thymus T cells learn self — those that react strongly to the person's own MHC markers are destroyed. Plasma cells (a) come from B cells; b describes a maturing RBC; d a basophil or mast cell.

34Lab 12Activity 4 · Innate vs adaptive
  • lab manual
  • textbook

In the lab's innate-versus-adaptive table, which row describes the adaptive response?

Answer: d

Adaptive — specific, days to weeks, memory present (B and T lymphocytes). Innate — non-specific, immediate (2–10 hours), no memory (barriers, phagocytes, NK cells, mast cells, complement, inflammation). Every other row mixes one column from each.

35Lab 12Activity 4 · Cell-mediated vs humoral
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

A bacterial toxin is circulating free in the plasma. Which branch of the adaptive response mainly deals with it?

Answer: c

Humoral (antibody-mediated) — against antigen free in the blood or tissue fluid: toxins and extracellular microbes. Plasma cells' antibodies neutralize it and flag it. Cell-mediated immunity is for cells — infected and cancer cells — that cytotoxic T cells kill (a). Helper T cells activate; they do not engulf (b). Memory B cells wait for a repeat exposure (d).

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend… you understand and know this table." — the table of adaptive-response cells (helper, cytotoxic and suppressor T cells, B cells, plasma cells, memory cells), Wed 11/18

36Lab 12Activity 4 · Cell-mediated vs humoral
  • lab manual
detail

According to the lab, a cytotoxic T cell recognizes its target by binding antigen displayed on which molecule?

Answer: a

The lab: TC receptor + CD8 bind antigen on MHC I of an infected or abnormal cell → perforins + granzymes → apoptosis. APCs present on MHC II to helper T (CD4) (b is the helper T's signal). Ch. 13 never names MHC classes and has the macrophage present to cytotoxic T cells too — this is lab material.

37Lab 12Activity 4 · Inflammation
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which two signs of inflammation both come from the same event — vasodilation raising blood flow to the area?

Answer: c

Histamine → vasodilation → more blood → redness + heat. Leaky capillaries → swelling (fluid and cells seep into the tissue). Pain comes from swelling pressing on nerves and from pain chemicals — bradykinins in the lab, prostaglandins in Ch. 13.

38Lab 12Antibodies
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Antibodies do not destroy antigens themselves. Which of these is NOT one of the antibody functions the lab lists?

Answer: d

The lab's five: neutralization, opsonization, precipitation/agglutination, complement activation, stimulation of inflammation — antibodies bind and flag. Perforins are released by NK and cytotoxic T cells. (Ch. 13's mnemonic PLAN gives four: precipitation, lysis via complement, attraction of phagocytes, neutralization.)

39Lab 12Adaptive immunity
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A breastfed infant is protected by antibodies in its mother's milk. What kind of immunity is this?

Answer: c

Passive — someone else's antibodies, immediate but short-lived, no memory cells. Natural — placenta or breast milk; artificial passive is injected antibodies (d). Active means making your own: natural from infection (a), artificial from a vaccine (b).

40Lab 12Activity 3 · Blood typingselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Going by the lab's blood-type table, which of these blood types carry anti-B antibodies? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b, c, d

A person carries antibodies to whichever ABO antigen they lack. Types O (no A, no B) carry anti-A and anti-B; types A carry anti-B only. B+ carries anti-A (anti-B would attack its own cells), and AB− has both A and B antigens, so its only antibody in the lab's table is anti-Rh. The Rh sign never changes the ABO antibodies.

41Lab 12Activity 4 · Innate vs adaptiveselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which statements about adaptive immunity are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, c, e

Responding the same way every time is innate immunity — non-specific, no memory (a). Adaptive immunity is specific and remembers, so a second exposure is faster and bigger (e). Helper T cells activate both B cells and cytotoxic T cells (b), and cytotoxic T cells killing infected and abnormal cells is the cell-mediated branch (c). Antibodies belong to the humoral branch, made by plasma cells (d).

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend… you understand and know this table." — the table of adaptive-response cells (helper, cytotoxic and suppressor T cells, B cells, plasma cells, memory cells), Wed 11/18

42Lab 12Antibodiesselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which are functions of antibodies? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b, d, e

Antibodies bind and flag; they destroy nothing themselves (c). The lab's list: neutralization, opsonization, precipitation/agglutination, complement activation and stimulating inflammation. Phagocytosis (g) and the oxidative burst (f), a chemical attack inside the phagocyte, are the phagocyte's work — opsonization only makes the antigen easier to engulf.

43Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cell ID
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On a stained smear, which cell is the one that, once activated, may become a plasma cell?

Answer: c — — a lymphocyte

A lymphocyte — small, with a round nucleus that nearly fills the cell. Activated B lymphocytes clone into plasma cells, which make antibodies. The kidney-shaped nucleus (a) is a monocyte, which becomes a macrophage — an antigen-presenting cell, not a plasma cell. The multilobed nucleus (b) is a neutrophil; the hidden nucleus under dark granules (d) is a basophil.

44Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cell IDselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

On a smear, which of these cells are granulocytes? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b, d

The granulocytes are the basophil (a), neutrophil (b) and eosinophil (d). The lymphocyte (c) and monocyte (e) are the agranulocytes — no visible granules. The trap is the basophil: its granules are so dense you cannot see the nucleus, but it is still a granulocyte.

45Lab 12Activity 3 · Blood typingselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which antigens and antibodies does a person with AB+ blood have? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, e

AB+ carries every antigen — A, B and Rh — and so no antibodies: a person cannot make antibodies against the antigens on their own red cells. That is why AB+ is the universal recipient. An Rh+ person never makes anti-Rh (d). There is no "O antigen" or "O antibody" — type O simply lacks A and B.

46Lab 12Activity 3 · Blood typing
  • lab manual

Patient 1's card clumps in the anti-B and anti-D wells only. Patient 2's card clumps in the anti-A and anti-D wells only. Which statement is true?

Answer: c

Patient 1 is B+, Patient 2 is A+ (each well tests its own antigen; D = Rh). An A+ person's plasma carries anti-B, so Patient 1's B-bearing red cells would agglutinate in Patient 2 — not a donor (a). Both are Rh+, so neither makes anti-Rh (b). Read the wells as antigens present, then name the antibodies as the ones the person lacks the antigen for.

47Lab 12Activity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual
  • textbook

A spun hematocrit tube shows its three layers. Which layer holds the anti-A and anti-B antibodies?

Answer: a

Antibodies are plasma proteins (gamma globulins) dissolved in the plasma. The A and B antigens are on the red cells (c) — the classic mix-up is putting antibodies on the cells. The buffy coat (b) is white cells and platelets. The plasma is also the layer that shrinks with dehydration, which is why dehydration falsely raises the HCT.

48Lab 12Activity 2 · Erythrocytesselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statements about hemoglobin are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: b, d

Hemoglobin has 4 subunits (2 alpha + 2 beta), each with a heme whose Fe²⁺ binds one O2 — so 4 O2 per molecule, not 2 (a) and not 3 subunits (c). More hemoglobin means more O2 the blood can carry, so a low reading means anemia (b). It also carries some CO2 (and H⁺), bound at a site other than the iron (d); most CO2 still travels as bicarbonate.

49Lab 12Activity 4 · Innate immunityselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Which statements about microbes and pathogens are true? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, c, e

A pathogen is a microbe that causes disease — a small subset of microbes, so (b) is false. Ch. 13a's six kinds: bacteria, viruses, protozoans, fungi, parasitic worms, prions (a). Bacteria are everywhere and most are harmless (c); normal flora on the skin and in the gut are part of the first line of defense (e). Microbes are microscopic by definition (d).

50Lab 12Activity 2 · Blood cell linesselect all that apply
  • lab manual
  • textbook
detail

Which cells come from the same progenitor line as T cells? Select all that apply.

Answer: a, b

T cells, B cells and NK cells all come from the lymphoid line (lymphoid progenitors become lymphocytes). Neutrophils, mast cells and monocytes come from the myeloid line, along with red cells. Sources disagree: the lab and the immunology glossary put NK cells in the lymphoid line, but Ch. 13 §13.2 calls the NK cell "a third type of white blood cell" and never calls it a lymphocyte.

51Lab 12Activity 4 · Lymphoid organs
  • lab manual
  • lecture
  • textbook

The lab asks for the role of the bone marrow in the immune system. Which answer is right?

Answer: a

Red bone marrow contains the blood stem cells, so every immune cell — and every RBC and platelet — is made there; B cells also mature there. Filtering lymph (b) is the lymph nodes, T-cell maturation (c) is the thymus, and removing old cells (d) is the spleen — the lab's own lymphoid-organ match.

52Lab 12Activity 4 · Lymphoid organs
  • lecture
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

Which lymphoid organ is the body's largest collection of lymphatic tissue, and what does it take out of the blood?

Answer: b

Whalen (Mon 11/16): the spleen is the largest collection of lymphatic tissue, and it pulls old RBCs (about 120 days) and old platelets (about 7 days) out of circulation — the lab's "removes old, damaged cells from the blood." The thymus (a) is where T cells mature; lymph nodes (c) filter lymph, not blood; the marrow (d) makes blood cells.

In lecture: "…the largest collection of lymphatic tissue in your body is known as the spleen. Another one of those … to be asked about someday." — Mon 11/16

1Lab 12short answerActivity 1 · Hematocrit
  • lab manual

Describe the hematocrit procedure, label the spun tube, and calculate the HCT for a 48 mm column with a 20 mm red layer. Is the result normal?

Model answer

Blood is drawn into a capillary tube with anticoagulant, capped, and centrifuged; the heaviest parts are pushed to the bottom. Tube, top to bottom: plasma (straw-coloured, about 55%) · buffy coat (WBCs + platelets, under 1%) · packed RBCs (about 45%). HCT = (RBC volume ÷ total blood volume) × 100% = 20 ÷ 48 × 100 = 41.7%. Normal is female 37–47%, male 42–52%: normal for a woman, just under the male range. Low HCT suggests anemia; high suggests polycythemia, or dehydration, which falsely raises it.

Marks for the three layers in order, the formula, the arithmetic, and reading the result against the ranges. The lab's calculation question; the reason males run higher is asked by the lab but given by no course source.

2Lab 12short answerActivity 1 · Blood components
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Complete the lab's table: for plasma, the buffy coat and the erythrocytes, give the components and the functions.

Model answer

Plasma — water carrying electrolytes, glucose and amino acids, hormones, dissolved gases, wastes (urea), and plasma proteins: albumin (fluid balance), globulins (α, β transport; γ antibodies), fibrinogen (clotting). Function: transport. Buffy coat — leukocytes (defense against pathogens and abnormal cells) and platelets (fragments of megakaryocytes; clotting, hemostasis). Erythrocytes — biconcave, no nucleus, full of hemoglobin (4 O2 per molecule); carry O2 and CO2, live about 120 days.

One mark per portion for components and one for function. The plasma proteins with their three jobs are where most points are lost.

3Lab 12short answerActivity 2 · Adaptive cells
  • lab manual
  • textbook
said it’s on the exam

List and describe the functions of the cell types involved in adaptive immunity.

Model answer

B lymphocytes — receptors for one antigen; when activated, clone into plasma cells (make antibodies at once — humoral) and memory B cells. They can also act as APCs. Helper T (CD4) — recognize antigen on MHC II of an APC, then release cytokines (IL-2, IL-4, IL-5) that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells. Cytotoxic T (CD8) — recognize antigen on MHC I of infected or abnormal cells and kill them with perforins and granzymes (apoptosis) — cell-mediated. Memory cells (B and T) — long-lived; give a faster, bigger secondary response.

A mark per cell type with its job. The lab's Activity 2 question; the MHC and CD details are the lab's own.

In lecture: "I really feel like you should know this table right here. I highly recommend… you understand and know this table." — the table of adaptive-response cells (helper, cytotoxic and suppressor T cells, B cells, plasma cells, memory cells), Wed 11/18

4Lab 12short answerActivity 3 · Rh vs ABO antibodies
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Explain how Rh antibody formation differs from A or B antibody formation, and why it matters in pregnancy.

Model answer

Anti-A and anti-B are present without exposure — the lab says formed before birth, as large IgM; a person has antibodies to whichever ABO antigen they lack. Anti-Rh forms only after an Rh− person is exposed to Rh antigen (a transfusion, or fetal Rh+ cells entering at delivery or miscarriage), and it is a small IgG that crosses the placenta. So a first exposure does no harm, but in a later Rh+ pregnancy the mother's anti-Rh crosses and destroys the fetus's red cells — hemolytic disease of the newborn. RhoGAM prevents it.

The lab objective, verbatim. Marks for: no exposure vs exposure, IgM vs IgG, the placenta. Note the lab's own table lists anti-Rh for every Rh− type, which contradicts its text and Ch. 11; the explanation above is the text's.

5Lab 12short answerActivity 3 · Donor and recipient
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Explain why a patient with O− blood can donate whole blood to all blood types but can receive blood only from O−.

Model answer

Antigens are on the red cells; antibodies are in the recipient's plasma. O− red cells carry no A, B or Rh antigen, so no recipient's antibodies have anything to clump — O− can be given to every type. An O− person's plasma carries anti-A and anti-B, and anti-Rh (the lab's table; by Ch. 11 once exposed — and an Rh− person should receive only Rh− blood either way). Any donor cells with A, B or Rh antigen would be agglutinated — so only O− is safe.

The lab's own explain question. Marks for: no antigens → universal donor; antibodies to all three → can only receive O−; using the word agglutination.

6Lab 12short answerActivity 3 · Donor and recipient
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Your blood types as B+. List the types you could donate red cells to and the types you could receive from, and give the rule you used.

Model answer

B+ has B and Rh antigens and anti-A only. Rule: the recipient must have no antibodies to the donor's antigens. Donate to: recipients with no anti-B and no anti-Rh — B+ and AB+. Receive from: donors without the A antigen; B+ has no anti-Rh, so Rh does not matter — B+, B−, O+, O−.

The lab's "find someone you could donate to / receive from", made answerable on paper. A mark for each list and one for the rule.

7Lab 12short answerActivity 4 · Innate vs adaptive
  • lab manual
  • textbook

Compare innate and adaptive immunity: the cells and structures involved, specificity, response time and memory.

Model answer

Innate (1st and 2nd lines) — skin, mucous membranes and their secretions; phagocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, macrophages, dendritic cells), NK cells, mast cells and basophils; interferons, complement, inflammation, fever. Non-specific; immediate (2–10 hours); no memory. Adaptive (3rd line) — B lymphocytes and plasma cells, helper T, cytotoxic T, memory cells. Specific; days to weeks the first time; memory present, so the secondary response is faster and bigger.

The lab's four-row table. One mark per row; the cells row is where marks go.

8Lab 12short answerActivity 4 · Cell-mediated vs humoral
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What is the difference between the cell-mediated and the humoral immune response? Are they innate or adaptive?

Model answer

Both are adaptive. Humoral (antibody-mediated) — B cells, activated by helper T, become plasma cells that secrete antibodies against antigen free in the blood and tissue fluid (toxins, bacteria, free viruses); antibodies neutralize, opsonize, agglutinate, activate complement and stimulate inflammation. Cell-mediated — cytotoxic T cells, activated by helper T, recognize antigen on MHC I of infected or cancerous body cells and kill them with perforins and granzymes (apoptosis).

Marks for: both adaptive; antibodies vs cells that kill; free antigen vs infected cells.

9Lab 12short answerActivity 4 · Inflammation
  • lab manual
  • textbook

What causes inflammation? Explain why it is characterized by redness, swelling, pain and warmth.

Model answer

Any cell injury or infection: chemicals from damaged cells make mast cells (the lab adds macrophages) release histamine, with serotonin and bradykinins. Redness — histamine causes vasodilation, so more blood flows in. Warmth — the extra blood heats the area, speeding metabolism and healing. Swelling — histamine makes capillaries leaky, so fluid and immune cells pass into the tissue. Pain — swelling presses on nerves, and pain chemicals stimulate pain receptors: bradykinins (lab) / prostaglandins from injured cells (Ch. 13). Macrophage cytokines then call in more cells to clean up and heal.

The lab's graded explain question; one mark per sign with its cause. The sources differ on pain: the lab names bradykinins acting on nociceptors; Ch. 13 names fluid pressure, bacterial toxins and prostaglandins. Naming both is safe.

% of blood that is RBCs = RBC height ÷ total height × 100. Female 37–47%, male 42–52%.
